articles.title_orig: Asia’s Buffers Too Thin to Keep Absorbing Oil Shock: World Bank
articles.title_zh: Asia’s Buffers Too Thin to Keep Absorbing Oil Shock: World Bank
articles.content_orig:
Photographer: Dario Pignatelli/Bloomberg
(Bloomberg) Economies in East Asia and the Pacific risk running out of firepower as they try to cushion the blow from an energy shock that’s set to persist into next year, according to the World Bank.
The region’s governments have responded more aggressively than peers elsewhere as the US-Iran war drove global prices up, and they’ve relied more heavily on subsidies, the World Bank said in its East Asia & Pacific Economic Update released on Tuesday.
The approach may be “unsustainable,” it said, forecasting that Middle East oil exports won’t return to pre-conflict levels until mid-2027. “These measures may postpone the adjustments to behavior required if the shock is persistent rather than temporary, while also imposing fiscal costs and lowering foreign currency reserves.”
The World Bank cited Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam, which have all taken steps to suppress retail gasoline prices and have seen their dollar war chests depleted by between 15% and 40% this year.
For now, energy risks are outweighed by what the bank calls the “AI tailwinds.”
It forecasts growth of 4.5% this year in East Asia and the Pacific, revising the figure up by 0.3 percentage point from the last forecast. That’s largely due to strong investment and exports led by the artificial-intelligence boom. The outlook for 4.4% growth next year was unchanged.
A longer-lasting energy shock could put more of that resilience at risk, especially if coupled with a downturn in the AI cycle and El Niño weather disruptions, the World Bank said. Higher energy costs have already weighed on manufacturing, while the surge in transport prices has hit consumer demand.
“A renewed rise in energy prices may be more damaging to economic activity than initially observed, particularly as the drag from higher inflation and tighter financial conditions grows,” it said.

articles.title_orig: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.title_zh: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.content_orig:
Trump: US "had a threat" that led to withdrawal of bombers at RAF Fairford
President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.
Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford?
What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites?
Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who.
The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.
One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.
US media outlets the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and Axios reported that the potential attack may have been designed to target the aircraft and kill personnel, citing unnamed officials.
The BBC has contacted the White House and the Ministry of Defence for comment.
Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men , Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.
Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency.
However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.
The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

articles.title_orig: Scandal-scarred televangelist Jim Bakker dead at 86: ‘Finished his race with faith’
articles.title_zh: Scandal-scarred televangelist Jim Bakker dead at 86: ‘Finished his race with faith’
articles.content_orig:
Disgraced televangelist Jim Bakker, who was as known for his scandals — including a $279,000 hush-money settlement to his church secretary — as he was his preachings, has died, his widow announced Monday. He was 86.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” Lori Bakker wrote on “The Jim Bakker Show” Facebook page .
“For 66 years, Jim gave his life to preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry.”
Bakker rose to prominence after founding “The PTL Club,” a Christian television show he co-hosted with his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, from 1974 to 1989.
The couple’s multimillion-dollar South Carolina empire included the PTL Satellite Network, a Christian cable platform, and the Heritage USA theme park, which drew millions of visitors before shuttering in 1989.
But the kingdom crumbled in 1987, after a $279,000 hush-money payment Jim Bakker made to church secretary Jessica Hahn came to light. She accused the popular preacher of raping her in 1980.
Bakker denied the rape allegations — though he admitted to having sex with Hahn, insisting it had been consensual.
“Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world,” Lori Bakker’s statement added.
“Our family is grieving and we ask for your prayers and privacy during this time. Jim finished his race with faith. His voice, his vision, and his legacy will never be forgotten.”
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.title_zh: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.content_orig:
It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?
T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”
I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.
Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan.
Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh.
And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”.
For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come.
Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.”
While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque.
It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs.
It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer.
Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.”
The prettiness of Le Butter’s packaging has naturally made it a social media hit, which Leo describes as a double-edged sword. “Obviously, I’m grateful,” he says. “But it can also be overwhelming. The aim of the shop is to educate people beyond supermarket butter, and to serve the locals as well as the tourists. We can only do our best.”
This fetishisation of butter is still quite divisive. “When it comes to food styling, some of what they do looks cool,” says Seb Myers of the restaurant Planque in east London. “But when you see a mound of butter – all that extravagance for the sake of a photo? I’m quite squirrelly with food. Waste is my big thing.”
In restaurants, I’ve lost count of the time I’ve been served butter shaped into little salted coins or whipped into something dippable. Bread and butter are still one of the most valued moments in a good meal. And as Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential, “If you eat at any good restaurant, assume you’ve eaten a stick of butter.”
“That’s partly because it starts the meal,” says Myers, who takes his butter pretty seriously. “If someone serves you an ice-cold pat of butter, you know you’re not in for a good time”. His restaurant is a play on Parisian bistronomy, so “it’s in almost every dish”. They use Beillevaire butter demi-sel sprinkled with flakes, sliced and well tempered. He keeps it in “a cheese fridge for a week to slow-mature it”. For cooking, it’s Douceur de France (they get through 10kg a week in cooking alone).
Pravin Nayar runs Castle Farm restaurant in Somerset, and makes his own: “We like butter to be the hero product when we do supper clubs.” The key, he says, is how you serve it: room temperature, sprinkled with salt. “The way I see it, bread is just a spoon for butter.”
R emember when butter was considered bad? After all those anti-saturated fat health campaigns, consumption hit a historic low by the late 1990s, with the average Brit consuming just 2kg a year. The perception around it seems to have shifted, although with 50% saturated fat – and I say this with love – butter is not exactly a superfood.
“The heart-health advice hasn’t changed,” says Tracy Parker, a registered dietitian and an adviser for the British Heart Foundation. “If you’ve got high cholesterol, or your diet already leans heavily on saturated fat – think fatty meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits – then you should probably reconsider how much you’re eating and whether you could swap it for something like olive, avocado or nut oil.” Butter is fine in moderation, though. “A light scrape on your morning toast, and thinking about everything else you eat – you’re probably OK,” she says.
So why the cultural rehabilitation of butter in a health-fad-mad 2026? Parker thinks it has become tangled up with the anti-ultraprocessed-food movement. “UPFs have been linked to poor health including obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease,” she says. Whereas butter is seen as a preindustrial, farm-adjacent product. “People view butter as a natural food

articles.title_orig: New York state declares measles disaster amid resurgence of disease in US
articles.title_zh: New York state declares measles disaster amid resurgence of disease in US
articles.content_orig:
New York state has declared a disaster emergency over an outbreak of measles, as cases of the disease that had once been all but eliminated in the United States continue to rise .
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said on Monday that she was temporarily expanding the ability of health professionals to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said in a statement, adding that New York has recorded 108 cases of measles this year, as of October 3. The declaration will remain in effect through November 4.
Hochul’s announcement marks the first such declaration since measles cases began to tick up in 2025. She said that seven cases were recorded in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.
Hochul’s declaration says 92 cases have been recorded since July 15 in a handful of rural communities with insufficient vaccination rates.
Officials in neighbouring Pennsylvania also announced that the state has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, the largest outbreak in the US in the last three decades. Outbreaks have also been recorded in Texas, Utah, Ohio and South Carolina.
Health experts attribute the resurgence to a decline in vaccination rates below the 95 percent rate they say is necessary to prevent outbreaks.
Critics say the decline has been spurred by an anti-vaccination movement that has surged in popularity and gained advocates inside the administration of President Donald Trump , including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
The US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles by 2000, with the last outbreak of more than 1,000 cases occurring over several years in New York City in the early 1990s.
International officials from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) are set to meet in November to determine whether the US and Mexico will retain their measles-free status, or whether the public health designations will be updated.
“PAHO reiterates the importance of maintaining high and homogeneous vaccination coverage, strengthening epidemiological surveillance, and ensuring timely outbreak response, as essential pillars to halt transmission and sustain measles elimination in the countries of the Americas,” the organisation said in a previous statement.

articles.title_orig: Jim Bakker, Television Preacher Felled by Sex and Financial Scandals, Dies at 86
articles.title_zh: Jim Bakker, Television Preacher Felled by Sex and Financial Scandals, Dies at 86
articles.content_orig:
by JIM SALTER Associated Press
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful “The PTL Club” TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show “The Jim Bakker Show” there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” Lori Bakker said in a statement.
But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on “Saturday Night Live.” A theatrical movie on their lives, “The Eyes of Tammy Faye,” was released in September 2021.
At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers’ ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
Bakker was born in Muskegon Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.
They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children’s show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting “The 700 Club,” a Christian talk show.
Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. “The PTL Club” — PTL stands for “Praise the Lord” — became its signature show.
It hit its heyday in the 1980s, “The PTL Club” was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.
Sort of a Christian version of “The Tonight Show,” it featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.
The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s abundant makeup.
In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.
In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL’s finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.
At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, “On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand.”
Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.
Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.
Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched “The Jim Bakker Show” on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.
In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.
The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.
Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000
articles.content_orig:
Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country
Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.
Pennsylvania’s health department said Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents ⁠have died ⁠after ​contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.
Lancaster county, with sizeable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.
The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr over how to classify measles-related mortality.
Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.
Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.
“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”
In New York state, governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.
Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.
The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.
In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.
Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.
According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s . That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters.
The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status .

articles.title_orig: Trump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
articles.title_zh: Trump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
articles.content_orig:
Nidal Hasan sentenced to death by military jury in 2013 for carrying out deadly shooting attack at army base in Texas
Donald Trump has approved the execution by US army firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a social media post.
Hasan, who was an army psychiatrist, would become the first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.
Parnell said in a post on X that defense secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended – and President Donald J. Trump has approved – death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan”.
He added: “The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.”
Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the mass shooting at the Fort Hood base.
He chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defense attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.
Hasan, a US-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on 5 November 2009 at a medical facility in the sprawling military base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralyzed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack.
The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that Hasan had spoken online with the radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an al-Qaida propagandist and American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
Although US mass shootings are disturbingly common, they are rare at military facilities.
In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.
In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.
A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group.”
Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital before being shot dead by officers.

articles.title_orig: World Teachers' Day
articles.title_zh: World Teachers' Day
articles.content_orig:
World Teachers’ Day is held annually on 5 October to celebrate all teachers around the globe. It commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers , which sets benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions. The Recommendation concerning the Status of Higher-Education Teaching Personnel was adopted in 1997 to complement the 1966 Recommendation by covering teaching personnel in higher education. World Teachers’ Day has been celebrated since 1994.
It is a day to celebrate how teachers are transforming education but also to reflect on the support they need to fully deploy their talent and vocation, and to rethink the way ahead for the profession globally.
World Teachers’ Day is co-convened in partnership with the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International.
In 2026, the Day marks the 60th anniversary of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. Six decades on, as the Recommendation is being revised, new challenges have emerged for the profession, from digital technologies and climate change to inclusion, migration and displacement. These pressures affect several dimensions of the status of teachers: their symbolic status, when teaching is not sufficiently recognized or valued; their professional status, shaped by limited autonomy, support or voice in policy-making; and their material status, compromised by salaries, workloads and working environments that do not allow teachers to fully exercise their role.
Under the theme " Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures ," the 2026 edition will centre on reviewing the current challenges related to teacher status and the strategies to address them, calling on society and policy-makers to protect, promote and elevate that status.
The global celebration organized at UNESCO Headquarters will feature high-level discussions on protecting and advancing the status of the teaching profession, as well as the award ceremony for the ninth edition of the UNESCO-Hamdan Prize for Teacher Development.
Other celebrations will take place around the world.
Joint Message from Mr Khaled El-Enany, Director-General of UNESCO, Mr Gilbert F. Houngbo, Director-General of the International Labour Organization, Ms Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF, Mr David Edwards, General Secretary of Education International, on the occasion of World Teachers’ Day 5 October 2026.
"On this World Teachers’ Day, UNESCO, the ILO, UNICEF and Education International call on governments and partners to stand with teachers by advancing the status of the profession  and  ensuring  that  every  teacher,  everywhere,  is  empowered  to  help  build more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable societies."
5 October at UNESCO Headquarters, Paris, France

Sumter County High School celebrated Homecoming 2026 with a week filled with school spirit, fellowship, leadership, and Panther pride under the theme “A Different World: Celebrating Our Past, Embracing Our Present, Building a Brighter Tomorrow.”
The celebration culminated with the recognition of 2026 Homecoming Queen Destiny King and Homecoming King Ja’Micquel Solomon. Sumter County High School congratulates King and Solomon on being selected as this year’s Homecoming royalty and celebrates their achievement as a highlight of the 2026 Homecoming festivities.
On behalf of the Sumter County School Board, Mr. Jerry Sanders, Superintendent, and Sumter County High School, Mrs. Calandra Parker, Principal, the school welcomed students, families, alumni, and community members to the 2026 Homecoming celebration and expressed appreciation to everyone who helped make the week a success.
The SCHS Homecoming Court represented the Panther spirit, leadership, and diversity of student life at Sumter County High School. The court included Homecoming King and Queen candidates, class representatives, and representatives from Career Technical Student Organizations.
Homecoming King Candidates included Eddie Trey Black III and Justiz Hollis, while Jordyn Jackson and Shannon Jackson were Homecoming Queen candidates.
The court also recognized representatives from each class: ● Mr. Freshmen: Jaylen Dice ● Miss Freshmen: Kaylee McCoy ● Mr. Sophomore: Ashton Dice ● Miss Sophomore: Makenzie Cromer ● Mr. Junior: Tyler Chamber ● Miss Junior: Tamea Hawkins ● Mr. Senior: Kelvin Carson ● Miss Senior Class: Madelynn Dice
Career Technical Student Organizations were also represented on the 2026 Homecoming Court. The representatives included: ● Mr. FBLA: Eythan Sanders ● Miss FCCLA: Brianna Shelton ● Mr. HOSA: William Serrano Dominguez ● Miss HOSA: Esther Gary ● Mr. JROTC: Jaylen Myrick ● Miss JROTC: Iyonna Roberts ● Mr. FFA: Francisco Granado IV ● Miss FFA: Joslyn Huffstutler ● Mr. SkillsUSA: Jeremiah Brown ● Miss SkillsUSA: Candace Raven
The SCHS student body organized a variety of activities throughout Homecoming Week to build excitement and strengthen school spirit. Students participated in dress-up days, a dodgeball competition, a “Day Party,” and a Panther Nic on the lawn, while also campaigning for the members of the Homecoming Court.
The week’s festivities culminated with the Homecoming Parade and football game, bringing students, faculty, staff, families, alumni, and community supporters together for a celebration of Panther pride.
The SCHS Cheerleaders, Coaches, and Student Government Association extend their sincere appreciation to everyone who worked extremely hard to make Homecoming 2026 a success. Their dedication and teamwork, along with the enthusiastic participation of students and the support of the community, helped create a memorable Homecoming celebration.
Homecoming 2026 reflected the spirit of its theme, “A Different World”—celebrating the past, embracing the present, and building a brighter tomorrow. Congratulations to Homecoming Queen Destiny King, Homecoming King Ja’Micquel Solomon, and every member of the 2026 Homecoming Court for representing Sumter County High School with Panther pride!

British Airways has today unveiled new cabins arriving on its retrofitted A380s, marking a major milestone in one of the most extensive cabin refurbishment programmes ever undertaken by an airline.
From nose to tail, customers will experience a transformed A380 aircraft, featuring redesigned interiors, new seats in every cabin and upgrades to the onboard experience, all designed to deliver greater comfort and a more premium end-to-end journey at 35,000ft.
The first completed A380 is expected to enter service in the coming months, marking the start of a fleet-wide transformation and forming part of the airline's wider investment in the customer experience.
Sean Doyle, Chairman and CEO at British Airways, said: "This is a major milestone for British Airways and the future of our A380 fleet, marking one of the most significant transformations we’ve ever undertaken on any aircraft.
‘We've completely reimagined the customer experience, introducing new and updated seats in every cabin, all carefully considered to deliver greater comfort and an elevated customer experience.
‘At the heart of the transformation is our brand-new First suite, but this investment goes far beyond a single cabin. From redesigned interiors and upgraded dining to new amenities and service delivery, every detail has been thoughtfully designed with our customers front and centre, helping them to have a more seamless and memorable experience when they fly with us."
Customers travelling in Club World (business class), World Traveller Plus (premium economy) and World Traveller (economy) will benefit from brand-new seats and upgraded cabin interiors. Thoughtfully redesigned with customer comfort in mind, the airline’s herringbone design features throughout the cabins.
Every part of the aircraft has been refined, including galleys and stairways bringing a new look and feel to every space on board.
From seat details to galley finishes, the new interiors create a clear identity throughout the aircraft, building on the design concept first introduced to the airline's short-haul fleet in 2024 and now shaping the future of its long-haul cabins.
New cabins with added comfort in mind
World Traveller and World Traveller Plus
Customers in World Traveller (economy) will enjoy a refreshed experience, including larger entertainment screens, wider seats and upgraded bedding. The relaxing new pillows feature a contemporary herringbone pattern and additional filling for added comfort and support. Plusher blankets, designed for added warmth and comfort have also been introduced in British Airways’ signature blue with red Speedmarque detailing.
Customers travelling in World Traveller Plus (premium economy) will also benefit from a host of improvements designed to make every journey more comfortable and relaxing. Seats will feature larger in-flight entertainment screens and privacy wings, alongside brand-new bedding and pillows helping customers arrive feeling rested and refreshed.
Customers travelling in World Traveller Plus will receive a new reusable amenity kit, designed as a tote bag for onward travel and featuring a Dr.PAWPAW moisturising balm and travel essentials, including a dental kit, socks and eye mask*.
The A380 will feature an evolution of British Airways’ Club Suite (business class) showcasing a refreshed design with a contemporary colour palette inspired by the airline’s blue, red and cream accents. Shaped by customer feedback, the suite includes added storage, improved functionality and carefully considered features designed to make every journey more comfortable and intuitive.
The aircraft will feature the world’s largest business class cabin, including 106 Club Suite seats across the full upper deck. Spanning four distinct cabin zones, the carefully designed space will offer a more intimate feel, complemented by dedicated dwell areas, Club Kitchens and reimagined galley spaces that encourage customers to move freely and relax throughout the flight.
Customers travelling in Club World will also enjoy the airline’s latest amenity kits, available in four unique designs created by British artists, powered by art platform, Rise Art, and stocked with exclusive products from luxury British wellness brand, anatomē.
A defining feature of the retrofit is British Airways' new First suite, combining ultimate comfort and privacy with considered touches to create an elegant space for customers to relax and unwind.
Designed to evoke a modern luxury hotel feel, the airline’s First cabin combines home comforts with thoughtful British touches at 35,000ft. The seat has been brought to life by expert designers and world-class manufacturers from across Great Britain and Ireland.
For customers travelling together in the centre seats, the divider opens to create a shared lounge, while stowable tables allow them to enjoy ‘buddy dining’ with their travel companion.
British Airways has partnered with luxury British heritage house, Swaine, to create a bespoke unisex First amenity kit inspired by the heritage suitcases carried by early air travellers, available on board from 6 October**.
Available in two colours, royal blue and cream, the kit contains a selection of skincare products from Wildsmith, a high-performance skincare brand that supports skin health and wellbeing. The kit will include a bespoke Circadian Rhythm collection aimed at supporting hydration and comfort from day into night.
The products include a face mist, hand and body lotion, ceramide multi-balm, lip balm, face cream, and an overnight mask, all carefully curated to support hydration and rest at altitude.
Hotel-quality sleep at 35,000ft
Customers in First can relax under a brand-new woven day blanket, featuring an elegant herringbone design. The new blanket will be complemented by a navy-blue cushion with subtle detailing. The airline’s bespoke tartan will also feature on the new cool-touch fabric navy sleepwear, complemented by slippers, all available on board from 1 October.
When it's time to sleep, crew will prepare the suite with a luxury mattress, lightweight cotton duvet and newly designed pillow, carefully developed to offer the ideal balance of softness and support, helping customers secure a great night’s sleep and arrive feeling refreshed at their destination.
Restaurant dining in the sky
The airline’s refreshed First dining service offers customers greater choice, using fresh flavours and new dishes that reflect the best of British produce.
The new dining experience will be available across the airline’s entire long-haul fleet from 1 October. A new ‘From the Grill’ concept means customers can create their preferred meal from a selection of premium proteins including British roast rack of lamb, grilled salmon, sides and sauces, as well as a selection of Signature Mains for a more personalised dining experience.
For added convenience, a bespoke mini bar has been integrated into the new First seat, giving customers easy access to popular refreshments throughout the flight, including a selection of premium snacks and still and sparkling water.
The new dining experience is complemented by contemporary stoneware and fine bone china, bringing a refined, restaurant-inspired feel to every course. A dedicated beverage menu features premium Champagne such as Bollinger La Grande Année, alongside a curated gin selection, such as Classic Gin Tonic, Rosemary & Orange, Spanish Flair as well as 0.0% Gin & Tonic. Customers can also enjoy a refreshing Showerings triple vintage cider as refined alternative to wine.
Every detail has been carefully considered, from cutlery designed by Studio William to wine glasses developed in collaboration with Richard Brendon and internationally renowned wine expert, Jancis Robinson.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court grapples with case on holding Big Oil liable for climate change
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court grapples with case on holding Big Oil liable for climate change
articles.content_orig:
Type to search articles, cases, and authors.
Press ↵ to view all results.
The Supreme Court on Monday opened its new term by hearing arguments in a lawsuit filed in state court by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, seeking to hold two major energy companies responsible for their alleged role in climate change and its impact. After nearly two hours of debate in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County , it wasn’t clear whether a majority of the justices agreed with the energy companies that federal law prohibits Boulder’s claims. With Justice Samuel Alito recused from the dispute, a 4-4 tie would leave the ruling by the Colorado Supreme Court, allowing Boulder’s case to move forward, in place.
Monday’s argument was the latest chapter in an eight-year-old battle that began when Boulder filed a lawsuit in a state court in Colorado against two energy companies: Suncor, a subsidiary of one of Canada’s largest energy companies, which operates the only two oil refineries in Colorado; and ExxonMobil, the largest energy company in the United States. It is seeking compensation for some of the costs that it has incurred as a result of the alleged effects of climate change – for example, protecting its own property as well as that of its residents. Boulder contends that both energy companies have long deceived the public about the effects of climate change and the role of fossil-fuel products in creating those effects; it also contended that the companies played a role in climate change by producing, refining, and marketing fossil fuels.
After their efforts to move the case to federal court failed, the energy companies asked the state trial court to dismiss the case, but it turned down that request. The Colorado Supreme Court then agreed to decide whether Boulder’s state-law claims were trumped by federal law. It concluded that they were not, and its claims could go forward. The companies came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to weigh in, which they agreed in February to do.
Representing the energy companies, lawyer Kannon Shanmugam described Boulder’s claims as an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct.” The Constitution, he said, bars the application of state law to “certain inherently federal areas,” and the Supreme Court has long held that federal law governs interstate-pollution claims. Moreover, he added, a state cannot regulate out-of-state conduct “based solely on attenuated effects” that it might have within the state.
Chief Justice John Roberts appeared skeptical, however. He suggested to both Shanmugam and Sarah Harris, the principal deputy U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the energy companies, that it was not uncommon for lawsuits to be based on conduct that occurs outside a state but has broad “effects,” including within the state. He asked Harris “what makes this situation different from those” other cases in which the court allowed lawsuits to proceed in state court.
Harris answered that, unlike those lawsuits, Colorado would ban the production of fossil fuels anywhere in the country.
Roberts did not appear persuaded. “That’s a question of relief” for Colorado, “and what might be available,” he said. It did not, in his view, necessarily seem to go to the question of whether Colorado could bring the lawsuit at all.
Justice Elena Kagan also seemed dubious of the energy companies’ arguments. She told Shanmugam that Boulder’s “suit appears to be based on the old 1990s tobacco suits,” as well as more recent lawsuits against opioid manufacturers. Were those lawsuits also trumped by federal law, she asked?
Shanmugam pushed back, describing the tobacco and opioid lawsuits as different. He stressed that the injury at the center of Boulder’s case “is not suffered by the Colorado consumer in the traditional sense.” He then pointed back to the principle that federal law has traditionally applied to claims involving interstate air and water pollution.
Kagan remained doubtful, asking Shanmugam to point to the support for that argument in the text of the Constitution or federal law or in the Supreme Court’s cases. “Where,” she finally asked, “is the[re] anything for that?”
Representing Boulder, lawyer Kevin Russell echoed Roberts’ point, telling the justices that states have long had the power to provide court remedies for injuries that occur within their borders even when the conduct that caused those injuries occurred elsewhere. Applying state law, he said, has never been interpreted as projecting that law nationwide. And he emphasized that Congress has the authority to pass laws that preempt state laws if and when it wants to.
Russell faced tough questioning, however, from Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was the member of the court most supportive of the energy companies’ position. He pointed to a series of Supreme Court cases that, in his words, “make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law” unless Congress specifies otherwise. In Kavanaugh’s view, those cases mean that state law generally does not apply to claims like Boulder’s, and Congress could believe that interstate-pollution issues are federal issues – and that it therefore does not need to pass new legislation to say so explicitly.
Several justices expressed concern about the possibility that allowing Boulder’s lawsuit to go forward would open the floodgates to even more cases in other states around the country. Justice Clarence Thomas asked Russell to describe any principles that might restrict whom state and local governments could sue.
Russell cited constraints on a state’s jurisdiction over particular defendants and a constitutional doctrine (known as the dormant commerce clause) that bars states from discriminating against out-of-state defendants, among other things, as possible limiting principles.
That prompted Thomas to ask whether, under Boulder’s theory, state and local governments could also sue “large retailers” of fossil fuels.
Russell acknowledged that “[n]othing in our theory prevents that,” but he added that “when lots of people act together to cause widespread harm, it is not uncommon for multiple different defendants to be potentially liable.”
Justice Amy Coney Barrett also sought to test the limits of Boulder’s theory, asking Russell whether Colorado could pass a law that sought to cap greenhouse-gas emissions in the other 49 states as well.
Russell agreed that such a law would be prohibited and sought to distinguish that scenario from Boulder’s lawsuit. He emphasized that, with the lawsuit, Boulder wasn’t trying to directly regulate the energy companies’ actions. The lawsuit, he argued, “doesn’t prohibit them from engaging in the conduct.” Instead, he said, “[i]t requires them to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities by paying for some of the damage that those activities inflict.”
Shanmugam picked up on these concerns in his rebuttal, telling the court that the “breadth of Boulder’s theory here is astonishing.” Indeed, he suggested, it would mean that on an upcoming visit to Colorado, Boulder could sue him “for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change.” Moreover, he suggested, it would not be only state and local governments who could sue under Boulder’s theory, but “[a]ny individual who has suffered the effects of climate change.” “Climate change,” he concluded, “is certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it.”
However the court opts to resolve the case, the justices devoted relatively little time to whether the Supreme Court has the power to consider the energy companies’ appeal at all – a question that the justices had asked the litigants to address when they agreed to take up the case earlier this year. The National Hurricane Center designated a low-pressure area in the southwestern Gulf as Invest 92-L on Monday.
Invest is short for “investigation” and refers to a weather feature that the National Hurricane Center is investigating.
This means we can start getting more spaghetti computer models about this disturbance.
WESH 2 First Warning Weather Meteorologist Cam Tran said the area of interest could become a tropical depression by the end of the week.
The system has 30 mph winds and a minimum central pressure of 1010 mb.
The latest model tracks show a slight easterly shift. However, there is still a big spread in where this could possibly go if it develops.
For now, the system is still expected to remain weak and well west of Central Florida.
Wind shear is forecast to increase across the northern Gulf later in the week. This could prevent anything stronger from developing, keeping the season hurricane-free.

articles.title_orig: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.title_zh: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.content_orig:
A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.
The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.
The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.
Dozens quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.
Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.
The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.
Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.
Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.
The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles .
With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.
Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.
Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.
Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.
The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination , except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.
Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.
Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.
The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.
Evans, who wrote “ Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19 ,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”
Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”
WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.
People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.
There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.
“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”
For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.
Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.
In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “increasing” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally increasing”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: Trump says he will stop using US taxpayer funds for ads
articles.title_zh: Trump says he will stop using US taxpayer funds for ads
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has said he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television ads he has fronted, following bipartisan pushback.
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," he said Monday on social media.
Trump said it is "a rather standard thing to do" but that he has decided to pay for the "Patriotic Ads" himself and with money he raised through his MAGA Inc super political action committee.
The ads, which praise the president and his policies, drew criticism and questions over their legality due to laws against using government money for political ads.
There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning  Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the "deep state" and others he perceives as enemies.
In one ad, Trump says, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all".
The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections , when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump's approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing - and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress.
The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads "educational" and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements.
They've pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines.
But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies.
"It's difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president," legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC.
Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads.
"It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language 'paid for by the U.S. Government,' should not be paid for by the United States government," the measure reads.
The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle.
Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while "I like the message ... it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars".
Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads.
"I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," the Louisiana lawmaker said.

articles.title_orig: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.title_zh: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.content_orig:
Author: Br. Murray Bodo, OFM
Date Published: October 05, 2026
In declaring 2026 the year of St. Francis , Pope Leo has once again called attention to the depth and breadth of the world’s interest in St. Francis. In this, the 800th anniversary year of his death , Francis has emerged as a saint who is as relevant today as he was in his lifetime.
We live in a time of division and upheaval in the world, with wars cropping up in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, and with hateful rhetoric and divisive decisions that are separating people. The good among us are longing and praying for peace daily: peace in the world and peace of heart. We long for models and look to saints for guidance about how we are to live our lives. Again and again, we turn to Francis of Assisi as the Christian example of a peacemaker who found peace of heart and preached peace and good by embracing Jesus and His Gospel of Peace and Love. “May the Lord give you peace,” and “Peace and Good” were the two mantras that Francis uttered his whole life long.
Ours is also a time of turmoil in nature. Our climate is warming yearly, and the excessive human consumption and use of fossil fuels are damaging our planet. There is the feeling that we are pushing the envelope of what our climate can take of human neglect and abuse.
And again, it is Francis of Assisi who emerges as a model of what it means to embrace all of creation as our brothers and sisters through whom and with whom we make our way to God. For St. Francis, it is because of the Incarnation of God among us that all creatures are redeemed, all creatures are seen as good. Francis embraced all creatures and called them Brothers and Sisters; and towards the end of his life he sang one of the great poems of the Middle Ages and of all time, his “Canticle of the Creatures.”
“Laudato si, mi Signore,” St. Francis sings, “Praised be You, my Lord,” through Brother Sun and Moon and the Stars; through Mother Earth, our Sister; through Brother Wind and Air, Brother Fire and Sister Water. In so taking the four elements of Medieval Cosmology: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, and embracing them and praising God through, with, and in them, St. Francis was embracing all creatures of the earth and praising and thanking God for them.
St. Francis of Assisi is the patron of ecology. (Photo courtesy of Br. Octavio Duran, OFM)
What a program for a renewal of the earth! What a program for peace of heart and peace among people and all creatures. And in his pursuit of that program for a peace-filled world, Pope Francis turned to St. Francis’s “Canticle” for the title and framework of his encyclical “Laudato Si,” in which Pope Francis stated that the most pressing need of the environment today is to address the human and social roots of the ecological crisis. For example, the encyclical calls for an immediate transition away from fossil fuels because climate change disproportionately affects the poor. Also, the wealthy consume and pollute excessively while the poor suffer the gravest consequences of environmental degradation, often being denied basic human rights like clean water.
The deepest crisis identified by “Laudato Si” is the placing of technology and economic profit above all else. Therefore, the most critical need of the world today is a profound and spiritual change that would lead to a more integrated vision of human beings, of their life, and their relationship with nature.
What a universal patron saint for these profound changes in our times is St. Francis! It has been suggested that the month of October, the month of his passing, be dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi, who is already a universal icon of peace and love among us. Perhaps Franciscans could ask that favor of Pope Leo, could suggest that we need to be reminded every year of the gift we have in St. Francis for renewing relationships in our time: the relationship we have with ourselves, with others, and with the very planet we live upon. All people need to hear every year St. Francis’s Admonition to his brothers who would be peacemakers:
“The peace which you proclaim with words must dwell even more abundantly in your hearts. Do not provoke others to anger or give scandal. Rather, let your gentleness draw them to peace, goodness and concord. This is our vocation: to heal wounds, to bind what is broken, to bring home those who are lost.” (Legend of the Three Companions, 58)
This reflection was originally published on FranciscanMonth.org and is republished here with permission. articles.title_orig: How will post-reunification Taiwan be governed? Policy advisers map out plans
articles.title_zh: How will post-reunification Taiwan be governed? Policy advisers map out plans
articles.content_orig:
Mainland Chinese scholars discuss varying levels of autonomy for the island based on how reunification is achieved
Seven years later, the first proposals from a handful of the mainland’s leading research institutes have either been finalised or are nearing completion, the South China Morning Post has learned.
Rather than setting out a single fixed model, scholars involved in those studies told the SCMP there should be different scenarios based on how reunification was achieved, with peaceful reunification granting Taiwan the largest scope of autonomy under Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework for post-reunification governance.
“The earlier Taiwan engages in talks with the mainland, the more bargaining power it would have, and therefore the greater the space it would have to shape the terms. That is almost inevitable,” said Chen Xiancai, a Taiwan affairs professor at Xiamen University.

articles.title_orig: 'Brazen plot': Mansion-selling California realtor charged with spying for China
articles.title_zh: 'Brazen plot': Mansion-selling California realtor charged with spying for China
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A real estate agent in California was arrested at LAX for allegedly spying for China, U.S. officials said.
Wanying “Heather” Zhang, 34, was detained at the Los Angeles airport just as she was leaving for China Sunday. The Californian is charged with acting as an unregistered foreign national.
The charge comes after Zhang travelled with an associate, identified as “Individual 1”, to Seattle in September 2025, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court.
It is claimed that under the direction of Chinese officials, she conducted surveillance on a Taiwanese official’s relative, taking pictures and videos, and collecting vehicle plate details before passing it onto a handler.
While the FBI didn’t name the alleged target, the New York Post reported it was Lai Ting-yu, son of Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te and an American resident.
“She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection,” First acting U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said, adding she was due to appear before federal court in Los Angeles Monday.
The Taiwanese president’s son, an engineer in his 30s, lives with his wife and their U.S.-born young child. He works with the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips .
According to the criminal complaint, security camera footage showed Zhang and Individual 1 waiting outside Lai’s home in a rented SUV.
When Lai or his family members arrived, they “quickly sat up within a black SUV, took out what appears to be their phones, and held their phones out in a manner indicating that they were taking pictures or videos of the family”.
"If the PRC wish to obtain leverage over the president of Taiwan during any potential conflict," FBI special agent Kevin Holt wrote in the complaint, filed on 3 October, referring to China by its formal name, People's Republic of China, “the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful.”
Taiwan's presidential office described Zhang's actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the U.S. government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses ​the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of ​nations," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
Zhang’s husband Edric Ding, also a realtor, told CBS News Sunday he did “not know anything yet”. It was not immediately clear if she had an attorney.
China has yet to comment on the arrest. The country is observing the weeklong National Day holiday, during which government offices remain shut.
Lai ⁠and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan's separate identity from China, a stance that angers Beijing , which sees the island as its sovereign territory. Lai says that the people of Taiwan alone can decide their future.

articles.title_orig: Woman arrested, accused of spying on Taiwan president's son in Seattle for China
articles.title_zh: Woman arrested, accused of spying on Taiwan president's son in Seattle for China
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president's family for China.
Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president's son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China as an unregistered agent, Assistant U.S. State Attorney Bill Essayli announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.
Zhang was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and an attorney who represents her could not be determined. She was due to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.
Taiwan's Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te's relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president's son, saying that "this is a classic case of transnational repression."
"Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the "People's Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan."
China considers him a separatist and has called him a "destroyer of peace."
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.
