articles.title_orig: CNBC Daily Open: China shuts down record 670 banks, new worries over oil and AI
articles.title_zh: CNBC Daily Open: China shuts down record 670 banks, new worries over oil and AI
articles.content_orig:
China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country.
Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis .
Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report, which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less developed regions of the country.
The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, nonperforming loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles.
The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to systemwide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure.
The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added.
The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy.
China's gross domestic product grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.

articles.title_orig: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
articles.title_zh: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
articles.content_orig:
Zack Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of", after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
The Green leader said "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".
The motion defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
More than a dozen Labour MPs reported the Greens to the equality watchdog on Monday, saying it raised "serious questions".
A Green Party spokesperson said: "We remain committed to upholding our own Code of Conduct and our duties under the Equality Act, and to ensuring the Green Party continues to be a safe place for all members."
Nine Labour MPs have also referred the party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation.
Sussex Police has been contacted for comment.
It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion , which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813.
"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said.
The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.
Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it.
Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community".
In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party".
He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of."
He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all".
Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".
On Monday, a group of Labour MPs wrote two letters to the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) - organised by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp - raising concerns about the motion, and amendments to protect Jewish members attending Zionist synagogues being voted down.
"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter to the watchdog said.
The EHRC, which regulates equality law in Great Britain, previously found failings in how Labour handled antisemitism.
In a statement, the EHRC told the BBC it would "consider each complaint carefully" and had not at this stage launched an investigation.
It added: "We have guidance advising political parties on their responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010. Like all duty-bearers, political parties must comply with the Act and take steps to avoid discrimination."
The European Green Party, of which the Green Party for England and Wales is a member, released a statement on Monday saying it wanted to "unequivocally distance" itself from the motion.
The umbrella body said it would "immediately demand clarity" from the party's leadership on how they would protect Jewish people and self-determination.
Meanwhile, Green MP Ellie Chowns told Radio 4's PM programme she was "deeply saddened" the motion had become party policy but disagreed it was antisemitic, saying it was underpinned by "principled opposition to the actions of the Israeli government".
She suggested a review of Green policymaking processes was needed since "less than 1%" of the party's more than 200,000 members had participated in the vote.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni military says it has retaken Mokha and 'secured' Red Sea waterway
articles.title_zh: Yemeni military says it has retaken Mokha and 'secured' Red Sea waterway
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Yemeni military also said in a statement that National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes.
But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces have only reached the city's outskirts.
The Houthis said they had struck Riyadh's international airport and other sites, but did not comment regarding Mokha.
Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks and reiterated calls for the UN Security Council's permanent members to support Yemen's government.
Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating.
Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said "our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area".
Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.
Houthi-run media denied reports that government forces had also made advances in Dhubab.
The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.
Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces in Saudi Arabia in an invocation of their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry.
Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.
Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".
The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP.
On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.
The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.
In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram.
According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.
A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

articles.title_orig: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.title_zh: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.content_orig:
A teenager has lost a hand in a grenade explosion as the return of school protests in France sparked clashes with police.
The 15-year-old was seriously injured in the northern city of Lens on Monday. Unverified police reports said that he had picked up a stun grenade.
France had said it would close up to 500 schools as demonstrations over understaffed and rundown schools entered a third week. Critics have called for the authorities to temper their response to the protests amid claims of disproportionate police force being used against minors.
The youth, injured near the Auguste-Behal vocational high school, was taken to hospital in Lille. His life is not in danger, according to Pas-de-Calais prefect Francois-Xavier Lauch.
A police union source reported that the student appeared to have picked up a rubber sting-ball or ”de-encirclement” grenade, fired by riot police, in an attempt to throw it back before it exploded in his hand, the AFP news agency reported.
Public prosecutors said investigators have yet to establish whether the teenager picked up the device or whether it landed on him.
They have referred the case to police internal affairs, which is now engaged in six investigations into serious injuries that have occurred during the student protests.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray described the teenager’s injury as “humanly dramatic” but said he would not comment further until the circumstances were established. He said 190 students had been injured since the protests began.
The Lens incident has added to scrutiny of police tactics during the demonstrations. Amnesty International France has criticised what it described as disproportionate police force against minors, saying it was alarmed by reports of students being hit with batons and subjected to tear gas and rubber-bullet fire known as LBDs.
The rights group said many of those taking part were minors under 18 and called on authorities to ensure policing methods were proportionate and compatible with France’s human rights obligations.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”.
The Education Ministry said 589 schools had been disrupted on Monday, down from 735 on Friday, according to figures reported by Le Monde. Earlier estimates had suggested between 400 and 500 of France’s 3,700 high schools could be fully or partially closed.
Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide.
Geffray said on Sunday that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked during the protests, with 78 teaching staff injured.
Reporting from a high school in Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said students had set up a barricade in front of the building’s entrance using dustbins and fences.
“We’ve been talking to many of the students who have come out here, and what they say is that they are here to have their demands heard by the government. They say they are fed up with teacher shortages and often don’t have teachers for subjects like maths and English,” she said.
“They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added.
Unrest and confrontations were reported in several cities on Monday. News channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest, and a fire being set alight as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris’s 13th district, said a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks attacked her school.
While police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated, suspending classes, Zerbib said it was “very violent and happened very quickly”, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes.
Since September 28, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across the country and dozens have been injured.
Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while property damage costs are estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
Student unions have called for national demonstrations on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Oil gains as traders weigh Gulf tensions against strong Mideast exports
articles.title_zh: Oil gains as traders weigh Gulf tensions against strong Mideast exports
articles.content_orig:
Middle East oil exports have climbed back above levels seen before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, despite Tehran’s attempts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz and attack vessels.
Crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September, reaching between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day (bpd), according to provisional data from maritime tracking firm Kpler. Before the war, exports averaged about 18 million bpd.
This surge in oil exports from the region has so far largely been attributed to US ships shepherding tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with increasing ship-to-ship transfers that reduce the risks of being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones. Meanwhile, the fact that oil prices have remained high has been explained by analysts as the result of still-elevated insurance rates — driven by fears of Iranian attacks — and a market factoring in the possibility of a return to a hot war.
But a senior Kpler analyst last week offered a different explanation for the rise in oil exports at high prices. Gulf countries, she suggested, may be paying Iran to allow their oil through – potentially handing Tehran a significant portion of the value of the cargo.
Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas exports passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Does this explanation hold up, and what does it mean for the war and oil prices?
Michelle Brohard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, recently said some countries could be paying Iran for passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
“I suspect there is a toll that’s being paid, which is giving these ships safe passage,” she said in an interview last week with energy analyst Rory Johnston.
“I also suspect that these countries know that this is unsustainable from a perspective of [the] US escorting [ships], and also unsustainable from them paying Iran 10 percent of their cargo, or 20 percent of their cargo,” she added.
“So you’re starting to see like what I would call like a race to get out as much as possible, as quickly as possible before the war restarts.”
The claim has not been independently verified, and Brohard presented it as speculation rather than a finding backed by evidence.
But as early as March, the shipping journal Lloyd’s List reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had already imposed a “toll booth” system to control vessel traffic through the strait.
The Trump administration, during the course of the war, has repeatedly said Iran will not be permitted to charge a toll under any potential agreement with Washington.
Closure of the strait has caused global fuel costs to soar and has tested agricultural sectors across the world.
Oil is increasingly getting out of the Middle East, marine trackers report.
In the last week of September, the seven-day average climbed above the roughly 18 million bpd recorded before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February – the first time since the conflict started.
Kpler said crude exports excluding Iran had also recovered to at least 16.5 million bpd as an average over September.
The pattern of increasing oil exports has continued into October. Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company on Saturday announced that it had transported two million barrels of crude on a very ‌large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general said was the company’s first such operation in decades.
According to Kpler, “40 percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore”, with much of it flowing through Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates pipelines.
The export figures also include supplies moved through the Red Sea, which has become an increasingly important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Moreover, the Kpler figures exclude any vessels that may have crossed the key transit route with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
Iran, however, disputes suggestions that it has lost control of the waterway.
Senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi said on Sunday only three to four million bpd were travelling along a US-supervised route and described that amount as “negligible” compared with pre-war traffic.
Before the war erupted seven months ago, the strait routinely saw about 125 large commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships.
Oil prices have eased marginally as exports from the Middle East recover. Last week, the Group of Seven countries also announced a decision to release 100 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves.
But crude prices remain significantly higher than pre-war levels. Brent crude was trading at about $101.59 a barrel on Monday, down 0.71 percent, while US West Texas Intermediate fell 1.2 percent to about $90.05.
“Despite exports from the region resurging, much will depend, longer-term, on the security of energy supplies,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, noting that the “situation is still tense”.
“The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, with the attack on another tanker on Sunday keeping worries bubbling about the potential for further disruption to supplies, particularly if shipping companies become increasingly reluctant to risk sending vessels through the crucial chokepoint.”
On Monday, an oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was instructed by the IRGC to turn back or risk being targeted, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) group that monitors shipping traffic.
Academic Abdul Khalique says while Kpler analyst Brohard’s speculation that a transit-fee arrangement has been put in place may be “plausible”, it is best described as an “informal security mechanism rather than a formal maritime levy”.
“No public proof confirms a systematic, state-run Iranian toll system,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.
He said the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) safeguards transit passage through international straits, “rendering formal tolls legally dubious”.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that Brohard’s suspected scenario was “in part” possible.
“Everything appears to be happening under the radar in the Middle East, from the US convoying ships to Iran quietly charging tolls,” he told Al Jazeera.
In September, the US government also imposed sanctions on a digital assets firm, BitBank, that it said had been used by Iran’s Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority — a body set up by the country’s government to collect fees for allowing the safe transit of vessels through the strait — to transfer money to Tehran.
However, Beauchamp said the biggest challenge for oil exports was now what he called the “problem of shipping”.
“The shuttle system in the Gulf is doing wonders in getting oil out, but it requires plenty of ships, and that has pushed freight rates higher while also reducing supply beyond the region itself,” he added.
According to Beauchamp, Asian buyers are having to find crude from further away too, “lengthening transit times”.
“Previously a supply story, this is now one about the underlying mechanics of shipping. While less exciting, it is arguably much more important and trickier to solve,” he said.
“Ships don’t get built overnight.”

articles.title_orig: Jeffrey Archer, Novelist Whose Real Life Rivaled His Thrillers, Dies at 86
articles.title_zh: Jeffrey Archer, Novelist Whose Real Life Rivaled His Thrillers, Dies at 86
articles.content_orig:
Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Monday.
Archer sold over 300 million copies worldwide and was known for pacy thrillers like his 1976 debut “Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less” and 1979’s “Kane & Abel.” His final novel, “Adam and Eve,” is due to be published on Tuesday.
Kate Elton, HarperCollins’ UK CEO and Archer’s editor, said in a statement: “We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend.”
Archer was also a prominent Conservative politician, who briefly served as a lawmaker before becoming a senior party official under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.
But he was as well-known for his very public downfall.
In 1987, Archer sued the Daily Star tabloid for saying he had paid a woman for sex, winning a then-record £500,000 ($660,450) in damages. The case returned to the public eye when he was selected as the Conservative candidate to become London’s first elected mayor in 1999. A former friend accused him of lying and Archer was eventually charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, convicted and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. He served two years, during which time he wrote “A Prison Diary.”
The trial of Archer’s libel case, which was heard in front of a jury, became notorious for the judge’s summing up of evidence given by Archer’s wife Mary.
“Remember Mary Archer in the witness box,” the judge, Bernard Caulfield, told the jury. “Your vision of her will probably never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance?”
And, of Archer, he added: “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel?”
Archer’s reputation as one of the most colourful figures in British public life did no harm to his literary career. His books were sold in 119 countries, HarperCollins said. He spent a total of five-and-a-half years on the New York Times bestseller lists.
He was due to speak about his final novel this weekend at the Cheltenham Literature Festival and had recently appeared on radio shows to promote the book.
HarperCollins said he had died suddenly and peacefully, “between writing sessions.”

articles.title_orig: ‘World Without Cows’ documentary coming to theaters
articles.title_zh: ‘World Without Cows’ documentary coming to theaters
articles.content_orig:
Film explores complex relationship between food, sustainability, biodiversity and people’s livelihoods.
The “World Without Cows” documentary is coming to theaters in the U.S. this October. After a five-year journey to bring this film to life, this is a big moment to experience it on the big screen.
The first showing will be Oct. 9 at the AMC River East 21 in Chicago, Ill., which will be attended by filmmakers Michelle Michael and Brandon Whitworth and executive producer Dr. Mark Lyons. Shows are also scheduled on Oct. 14 at select theatres in Illinois, Wisconsin, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kentucky, Nebraska, Texas, Minnesota, North Dakota and Pennsylvania. Find participating theaters, showtimes, ticket information and more about the theatrical release on the "World Without Cows" website . More theaters are being added daily.
Make a night of it, and bring your crew. Bring your family, friends and colleagues to fill theaters across the U.S. with people ready to rethink the role of cows in the future of our planet. Sold-out showings can lead to a broader theatrical release, and the simple act of you and your network showing up is powerful support of “World Without Cows.”
Related: Packers, imports and profit: “Are you sure about that?”
Cows are tied to some of the biggest questions facing humanity: how we feed a growing population, protect the planet and provide adequate nutrition in communities around the world. Against a backdrop of climate change, food insecurity and rising protein demand, “World Without Cows” challenges what we think we know about cows, climate, health and the future of our planet. Through a global journey spanning 22 countries and five continents, the film explores the complex relationship between food, sustainability, biodiversity and the people whose lives hang in the balance.
Award-winning journalists Michelle Michael and Brandon Whitworth spent five years filming in more than 40 locations, in conversation with farmers, ranchers, scientists and environmental experts. What they found was far from simple: When it comes to cows, it's not black and white.
“The journey showed us that there is no single simple solution to the world’s greatest challenges,” said filmmaker Michelle Michael. “I don’t think the world wants simple answers. It wants a better understanding of how our global food systems work, and that need has never been more urgent than it is right now.”
“Our hope is that ‘World Without Cows’ creates a new baseline for how people engage in hard conversations,” said filmmaker Brandon Whitworth. “The film wasn’t made to be an echo chamber. It was made to bring people together to ask difficult questions about complex issues and be open to different perspectives.”
Related: Meat Institute celebrates 120th anniversary
"Cows have become a symbol in the climate conversation, but the reality is far more complex. By exploring this issue from many angles and in such diverse geographies, the filmmakers give us a much more insightful and hopeful outlook than we might have expected," said executive producer Mark Lyons.
For more information, visit https://worldwithoutcows.com .

articles.title_orig: Child mortality has declined in all world regions
articles.title_zh: Child mortality has declined in all world regions
articles.content_orig:
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy .
In 2025, the amount of foreign aid given by the world’s richest countries fell by almost a quarter . That amounted to a reduction of roughly US$50 billion.
Aid cuts in the United States — and the shutdown of its agency for international development, USAID — got the most attention, and for good reason: the US is the world’s largest aid donor in dollar terms, so its contributions make a huge difference to the global total.
But many other countries cut their aid contributions, too. In the chart, you can see the change among the largest 10 donors (in dollar terms) from 2024 to 2025. This is given as a share of their gross national income.
Contributions fell in eight of the ten countries. Only Sweden and Italy increased their budgets.
The countries shown are the largest donors in dollar terms; some others not shown contribute far more in relative terms: Norway, for example, was the only country to give more than 1% of its national income to foreign aid.
If your job was to sell cars in Turkey in 2022, selling an electric one would be an unusual day at work. Just one new car out of every 100 sales was electric.
By 2025, this had become a fairly normal day. More than one in five new cars were electric — a more than 20-fold increase in just three years. You can see this rapid takeoff in the chart.
Why did electric models become so popular? In 2023, the government introduced tax relief for electric cars, cutting the registration tax compared to petrol and diesel cars. This was timed to coincide with the launch of Turkey’s first domestic electric car manufacturer, Togg , which has quickly become the market leader. Imports of cheaper electric car models, including from China, have also made these markets more diverse and cost-competitive.
This combination of factors has made electric cars far more affordable than they were just a few years ago.
We are all surrounded by nickel. It’s one of the key ingredients in stainless steel, so most of us see it every day: from the pots we cook with, to the pipes in bathrooms, the batteries in mobile phones, and alloys in cars.
For nearly four decades, Indonesia — which has the world’s largest reserves — mined nickel but processed very little of it at home. This changed around a decade ago, when the government banned the export of raw nickel, forcing companies to process it domestically.
That’s the focus of the chart, which shows processed nickel production in tonnes among today’s largest producers.
Indonesia’s production increased more than 60-fold, going from around 22,000 tonnes in 2014 to over 1.4 million tonnes in 2023. The country went from producing 1% of the world’s total processed nickel to 41% in that period.
In 2021, Indonesia overtook China to become the world’s largest producer and is now far ahead. But much of that growth involved Chinese capital. The International Energy Agency reports that Chinese companies now own the vast majority of Indonesia’s nickel refining assets.

articles.title_orig: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.title_zh: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.content_orig:
When we think of viruses, we often associate them with disease, but many viruses in nature have nothing to do with human illness.
A new study that included Clemson University microbiologist Barbara Campbell suggests that one poorly described group in particular — giant viruses — may be important participants in ecosystems ranging from ocean and freshwater systems to soil.
A collaborative international research team created the largest catalog yet of giant virus genomes. The collection includes 18,727 metagenome-assembled genomes, which are genetic reconstructions made from environmental samples from marine and freshwater systems, soil, rock, thermal springs, plant-associated environments and landfills.
After comparing the genomes, the researchers identified 8,508 species-level representatives, 712 previously unknown genera, 13 new viral families and a proposed new order called Mycodnavirales .
The study, published in the journal Nature Microbiology, provides new clues about the diversity and possible ecological roles of giant viruses.
“We’re interested in what’s going on out there in the environment at the microbial scale,” said Campbell, much of whose research involves the Chesapeake and Delaware bays .  Her group is especially interested in the ecological questions of “Who’s there? What are they doing? What and who are they interacting with?”
The study uses metagenomics to help answer those questions.
Most of the microbes in marine and estuarine environments are difficult to grow in the laboratory, and studying viruses depends on host cells. With metagenomics, scientists collect an environmental sample and sequence all the DNA in it. The genetic material comes from many organisms, and researchers use bioinformatic tools on high-performance computers such as Palmetto to assemble the fragments into larger sequences that can reveal the organisms’ identities.
“It allows us to look to see what’s in the environment without actually having to culture it,” Campbell said.
Despite their name, giant viruses can’t be seen by the human eye.
“They are giant, but giant is relative,” Campbell said. “You still need a microscope to see them.”
Bacteria are huge when compared to viruses. The smallest bacteria are about 0.4 microns in diameter, or one millionth of a meter. Viruses range in size from 0.02 to 0.25 microns. Most viruses are submicroscopic, meaning they are unable to be seen in an ordinary light microscope. They are typically studied with an electron microscope.
But some giant viruses are nearly the size of bacteria, and their genomes can exceed 2.5 million DNA base pairs. They may have hundreds of thousands of genes, including genes related to metabolism and protein production. That genetic complexity gives giant viruses the potential to influence the cells they infect in unusual ways.
Some giant viruses carry genes associated with producing proteins, a process other viruses leave to their hosts. Others contain genes connected to metabolism, stress responses and cell signaling.
“A lot of them have most everything needed to sustain life,” Campbell said.
That doesn’t mean they live independently. They still need host cells to reproduce. But their large genomes may allow them to manipulate host cells in more complicated ways than smaller viruses can.
According to the study, researchers found potential clues about the environmental roles of giant viruses, too. For instance, some groups contained genes associated with processing formaldehyde and breaking down aromatic compounds, including substances that can occur in industrial pollution.
The giant viruses in the study are generally host-specific and are not expected to infect humans. However, their impact could be felt by humans because they may help shape the health of oceans, bays, lakes and soil.
For Campbell, the results reinforce how much scientists still do not know about the smallest life forms in oceans and estuarine waters.
Viruses are part of what scientists call the microbial loop. Many giant viruses infect microscopic organisms such as phytoplankton and protists. When viruses break open their hosts, nutrients inside the cells are released back into the environment where they can be used by other organisms.
In low-nutrient marine and estuarine environments, that recycling can be especially important. Estuarine and marine phytoplankton are essentially single-celled plants that absorb carbon dioxide and produce roughly half the Earth’s oxygen she said.
“So knowing more about what makes them tick, and how they survive and die, is important, and studies like this give us an excellent starting point,” Campbell said.

articles.title_orig: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate
articles.title_zh: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate
articles.content_orig:
Jorge Dubcovsky, a wheat geneticist at the University of California, Davis, has been named the 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate in the category for countries with developed economies.
The award recognizes his contributions to wheat improvement and global food security. It is presented by the Global Confederation of Higher Education Associations for the Agricultural and Life Sciences, known as GCHERA.
Dubcovsky is a distinguished professor in the UC Davis Department of Plant Sciences and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute researcher, according to a press release.
For more than three decades, Dubcovsky’s research has advanced understanding of wheat biology and helped breeding programs apply genomic tools to crop improvement.
His work has identified and characterized genes controlling yield, disease resistance, flowering time, nutrient use efficiency and adaptation to different growing environments. Those discoveries have contributed to improved wheat varieties grown on millions of hectares worldwide.
“The World Agriculture Prize recognizes individuals whose achievements have had a profound and lasting impact on global agriculture and human well-being,” said Doug Steele, chair of the World Agriculture Prize International Committee. “Dubcovsky’s scientific leadership and extraordinary contributions to wheat genetics have strengthened the resilience of one of the world’s most important food crops and have delivered tangible benefits to farmers, food systems and society. His work exemplifies the innovation, excellence, and global impact that the prize seeks to honor.”
Dubcovsky has worked with researchers, breeding institutions, governments and international agricultural organizations to move wheat discoveries into practical use. He has also mentored plant scientists and breeders who continue to contribute to crop research and development.
The World Agriculture Prize recognizes contributions to agriculture and food security through research, innovation, leadership and service. GCHERA also recognizes scientists from countries not classified as having developed economies.
Dubcovsky will be formally honored Oct. 28 at the 2026 World Agriculture Prize Award Ceremony at Nanjing Agricultural University in China.
_src_links: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate

articles.title_orig: Dennis Hastert, the disgraced former US House speaker who went to prison, dies at 84
articles.title_zh: Dennis Hastert, the disgraced former US House speaker who went to prison, dies at 84
articles.content_orig:
J. Dennis Hastert rose from a rural high school wrestling coach to the heights of power as the longest-serving Republican speaker of the U.S. House before an ignominious fall and imprisonment amid revelations he sexually abused youths he had coached.
Once the third-most-powerful elected official in the country, serving as speaker from 1999 until 2007, Hastert died Sunday of natural causes at his home in Plano while under hospice care, Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell said. He was 84.
His death came a decade after he was sentenced to 15 months in prison for illegally structuring $950,000 in bank withdrawals to evade federal reporting requirements. The money was for hush payments to one of his victims, identified in court only as Individual A.
Hastert’s admission in court that he had sexually abused several boys he coached on the Yorkville High School wrestling team in the 1960s and 1970s left him living a life largely “isolated from society,” one of his attorneys said. Friends who had encouraged his rise in national politics and celebrated him as a local hero shunned him.
It was a stunning fall for a politician hailed across party lines in Illinois, where many colleagues knew him not as “Mr. Speaker” but as “Denny” or simply “Coach.”
For the family of one of his victims, his death brought little relief.
“I thought I would feel more relief and kind of a final closure, and I do, but nothing changes the fact that I lost my brother and I believe he had a lot to do with it,” said Jolene Burdge, whose brother, Stephen Reinboldt, told her Hastert abused him throughout high school. Reinboldt died years before the allegations against Hastert became public.
John Dennis Hastert III’s political career was yet another example of the important role that timing plays in politics.
After serving as a teacher and wrestling coach at Yorkville High School in the mid-1960s, he led the team to a state title in 1976 and earned coach-of-the-year honors. In 1980, he ran for the Illinois House and finished third in a Republican primary challenge to state Rep. Al Schoeberlein. But months later, Schoeberlein became terminally ill, and local party leaders chose Hastert to replace him on the ballot.
Six years later, similar circumstances occurred when U.S. Rep. John Grotberg, who had frequently battled cancer, became incapacitated around the time of the primary election. Hastert’s supporters helped engineer his nomination from among a field of 12, and he headed to Congress.
A conservative with a strong Christian background from his years attending Wheaton College, Hastert opposed the Equal Rights Amendment and abortion. But as chief deputy whip, he was known for bridging differences between the GOP’s conservative and moderate factions.
That skill proved valuable in 1998, when House Speaker Newt Gingrich stepped down after disappointing Republican losses in the midterm elections. In mid-December, Speaker-designate Robert Livingston of Louisiana took to the floor and made a surprise announcement that he was withdrawing after revelations of his extramarital affairs became public.
Within hours, Hastert secured enough Republican votes to win the post and was dubbed “the accidental speaker.”
As speaker, Hastert strongly supported President George W. Bush’s domestic and foreign agendas. In 2004, he formalized what became known as the Hastert Rule, under which only legislation backed by a majority of House Republicans would get a floor vote.
He also was a strong supporter of “earmarks,” federal projects sought by individual members that were often derided by critics as “pork barrel” spending. The Washington Post found that between 1999 and May 2005, Hastert directed $24 million in grants to groups in Aurora, his birthplace.
Perhaps his most notable earmark was $207 million to start the 37-mile Prairie Parkway project that created a north-south expressway connecting Interstates 88 and 80 in the far west exurbs. Hastert never revealed that the highway’s construction would benefit a land investment he and his wife had made. Months after Bush signed the 2005 highway bill into law, a land sale netted the Hasterts nearly $2 million, but the speaker denied any wrongdoing.
Federal funding for the project, which was opposed by local residents, was rescinded in 2012. In 2018, the Illinois Department of Transportation abolished a protective corridor that had been established for it.
After Republicans lost the House in the 2006 midterm elections, Hastert stepped down from GOP leadership and later resigned his seat in November 2007 to become a consultant and powerful lobbyist.
Five years later, the FBI began looking into Hastert and large cash withdrawals he was making from local banks in amounts just under $10,000, the threshold that triggers reports to federal regulators.
At first, federal investigators said Hastert told them he didn’t trust banks and then said he was a victim of an extortion scheme — lies that led to his prosecution.
Agents then learned he had sexually abused youths he coached, including Scott Cross, the brother of former Illinois House Republican leader Tom Cross. Tom Cross had been a protege of Hastert and a member of his political operation.
Hastert was indicted in May 2015 by a federal grand jury. After a plea agreement, U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin sentenced him in April 2016 to 15 months in prison, repeatedly calling him a “serial child molester.”
“Nothing is more stunning than having the words ‘serial child molester’ and ‘speaker of the House’ in the same sentence,” Durkin said.
In all, five former students came forward to accuse Hastert of sexual abuse. Prosecutors said the abuse occurred in empty locker rooms and motel rooms on summer wrestling trips, often predicated by Hastert offering a massage. Victims also told authorities that Hastert would pull up a reclining chair after practices and watch the boys shower.
Hastert reported to the Federal Medical Center in Rochester, Minnesota, on June 22, 2016, a little over a year after his indictment. He served about 13 months of his 15-month sentence before being placed on supervised release. Because Hastert admitted he abused boys as a wrestling coach, he also was ordered by a judge to take part in a sex-offender treatment program, including any “psychological and physiological testing” recommended by his probation officer.
In 2021, years after Hastert’s release, a lawsuit filed by the man who was supposed to receive a total of $3.5 million in hush money payments was settled in Kendall County court, just days before it was scheduled to go to trial. The terms of the settlement were never made public, and Individual A was never identified in court.
Hastert’s portrait at the U.S. Capitol was removed from display and sent to storage. The National Wrestling Hall of Fame removed him in 2016. Wheaton College took his name off its public policy center, which still houses the congressional papers he donated.
Reinboldt, the wrestling team’s longtime student equipment manager until his 1971 graduation, died of AIDS in 1995 at age 42.
Burdge, his younger sister, who lives in Billings, Montana, said her brother told her Hastert had abused him “all through high school.” According to a court filing, three other people later came forward to say Reinboldt had also confided in them about the abuse.
At Hastert’s 2016 sentencing hearing, Burdge testified that her brother spent years “running from the pain and turmoil” caused by Hastert’s abuse and was afraid to speak out because he thought no one would believe him.
In an interview with the Tribune on Monday, Burdge said news of Hastert’s death had left her surprisingly emotional, and she had been tearful all day thinking about her brother and how Hastert’s actions ruined his life. She thinks of her brother often, she said, and Hastert’s death brings a finality to the sad saga.

articles.title_zh: When the World Is Your Oyster: Aquaculture in the Age of Climate Change
articles.content_orig:
In the Ocean State, aquaculture—the farming and harvesting of primarily oysters, but also clams and quahogs—is a booming business. There are 89 individual aquaculture sites in Rhode Island, covering 392 acres of water, mostly in the state’s salt ponds. Oysters are the No. 1 aquaculture product in the state, with 11 million sold for consumption in 2024. The total value of the state’s aquaculture industry was $7 million.
This three-part series looks into whether pollutants such as PFAS in Narragansett Bay and Rhode Island's salt ponds are impacting shellfisheries and whether these stressors pose a risk to human health from consumption of shellfish . This project examines the economic vulnerability and viability of oyster farmers in light of rising seas, ocean acidification, and coastal development. This series also looks into regulatory blind spots and testing inconsistencies as well as new technology in oyster farming.

articles.title_orig: Alleged unregistered agent of China set to appear in court
articles.title_zh: Alleged unregistered agent of China set to appear in court
articles.content_orig:
An Irvine, Calif. woman accused of operating as an unregistered agent for China was scheduled to appear for arraignment in the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles Monday – one day after being arrested by the FBI at Los Angeles International Airport. Wanying Zhang, 34,…
A Decrease font size. A Reset font size. A Increase font size.
By Chris Woodward | The Center Square
An Irvine, Calif. woman accused of operating as an unregistered agent for China was scheduled to appear for arraignment in the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles Monday – one day after being arrested by the FBI at Los Angeles International Airport.
Wanying Zhang, 34, also known as “Heather Zhang,” was taken into custody by the FBI’s Los Angeles field office on Sunday as she attempted to board a flight bound for China.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli highlighted the arrest on X, noting that federal authorities intercepted Zhang before she could leave the country.
“We just arrested a Chinese foreign agent at LAX attempting to depart for China,” Essayli posted . “According to the affidavit, Zhang traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, at the direction of PRC [People’s Republic of China] officials, surveilled a close relative of a Taiwanese government official, sending photos, videos and license plate information to those officials.”
According to the federal criminal complaint, Zhang’s alleged operations spanned from June to September 2025 without notifying the U.S. attorney general, something that is required by federal law.
In a Department of Justice press release , investigators detail a calculated scheme utilizing specialized tradecraft to evade detection. For example, authorities believe that in June 2025, Zhang traveled from Southern California to China, where investigators claim she met directly with Chinese officials and received orders to conduct surveillance on U.S. soil.
U.S. authorities alleged that on Aug. 29, 2025, Zhang and an accomplice flew from John Wayne International Airport in Orange County to Las Vegas, later traveling to Washington state, where the victims reside.
DOJ also states that court documents show Zhang coordinated her travel with an associate, utilized counter-surveillance tradecraft and sent real-time updates to Chinese handlers — including a boarding pass photo, video footage outside the target’s residence, confirmation of spotting the target and vehicle license plate numbers.
Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, called the alleged actions a “brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil.”
Rozhavsky added that the case demonstrates the FBI’s commitment to defending democratic allies. Taiwan, an independent constitutional democracy, maintains that it is not part of the People’s Republic of China, despite Chinese claims that Taiwan is part of China.

﻿A rumored Android update would automate personal phone calls with Gemini AI.
Google may be expanding its “Call for Me” AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a “Gemini Calling” introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include “Call Mom and tell her I will be 15 minutes late” and “Call John and ask if he is coming for dinner.”
Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google’s AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or even still have a landline phone.
Android Authority also says it found “granular permissions” for Gemini actions in individual apps, including what appear to be settings for phone call permissions. These settings would allow users to pick and choose which app capabilities they want to allow Gemini to access, potentially giving users an option to opt out of receiving incoming automated calls from Gemini. However, as Android Authority notes, it’s also possible Google might not publicly release this expansion or the granular Gemini app settings.

articles.title_orig: John Thune says ‘no clear path forward’ for clock-change bill
articles.title_zh: John Thune says ‘no clear path forward’ for clock-change bill
articles.content_orig:
We've all done it: spring forward, fall back. But what if the clock never moved again?
Arkansans have mixed feelings about the nationwide debate over making daylight saving time permanent, and experts say the decision could affect more than our schedules.
"Some people think if we were to stay, they'd somehow lose that hour. Now the hour's still there," Arkansas Rep. Stephen Meeks (R) said.
The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act would make daylight saving time permanent, meaning Americans would no longer change their clocks twice a year.
The U.S. House passed the bill in July by a large bipartisan margin, but the legislation has stalled in the Senate. Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton is among the lawmakers opposing permanent daylight saving time.
"Daylight saving time is artificial," Meeks said. "The better choice would be to go on standard time and stay there year-round."
Meeks has also been involved in the debate at the state level. He pushed an Arkansas bill last year that would have kept the state on standard time year-round, but that bill died in committee.
RELATED: Arkansas lawmaker's attempt to end daylight saving time fails
One of the biggest concerns from opponents is what permanent daylight saving time could mean for winter mornings, particularly for children heading to school before sunrise.
"What ends up happening is our children are going to school in the dark, in the coldest, darkest, basically hours of the year, and it creates basically it creates a hazard for them," Meeks said.
That is also at the heart of Cotton's opposition. The senator has pointed to the possibility of much later winter sunrises under permanent daylight saving time.
In Little Rock, experts say winter sunrise could occur as close to 9 a.m. CT under permanent daylight saving time.
Congress has actually tried year-round daylight saving time before. The U.S. adopted it in 1974 to conserve energy, but Congress later restored standard time during the winter months.
Another piece of this clockwork is our bodies.
Dr. Ashtaad Dalal with the American Academy of Sleep Medicine said research has linked the spring transition to increased risks involving motor vehicle crashes, cardiovascular problems, stroke, heart attack, and mood disturbances.
"It simply shifts an hour of available daylight from the morning to the evening. So yes, would get more daylight after work and school, but you would pay for that with darker mornings, which we know are inherently dangerous," Dalal said.
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine said it supports eliminating the twice-yearly clock change but favors permanent standard time rather than permanent daylight saving time.
Supporters of permanent daylight saving time see it differently, arguing that eliminating the clock change would provide more evening daylight for work, school, sports and outdoor activities.
President Donald Trump has also pushed for permanent daylight saving time and recently urged people to contact Cotton to change his position.
For now, the legislation remains stalled in the Senate as lawmakers debate whether the country should keep the clocks from changing, and which hour of sunlight Americans should keep.
"We should be looking for policies that support healthy sleep, not policies that work against our biology," Dalal said.
We at THV11 did learn that Sen. Cotton has the power to put the bill on hold. We will continue to gather updates as we head into election season, with Congress heading home to prepare for Nov. 3 midterms.

articles.title_orig: A lawsuit accuses Starbucks of mislabeling 8 ‘sugar-free’ protein drinks
articles.title_zh: A lawsuit accuses Starbucks of mislabeling 8 ‘sugar-free’ protein drinks
articles.content_orig:
Illuminated Starbucks logo in the window of a Manhattan store, New York, New York, September 29, 2026. (Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
That Starbucks protein drink labeled "sugar-free" on the coffee chain’s menu may really have more sugar than a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, a new consumer lawsuit claims.
The federal lawsuit, which was filed on behalf of three consumers, claims the Seattle coffee chain promotes the protein drinks as sugarless despite the fact that they do contain sugar. The plaintiffs allege that Starbucks’ naming and marketing of the beverages are "false, deceptive, and unlawful."
As of Monday, Starbucks listed the drinks on its U.S. website under a "No Added Sugar Options" header with each of the beverages containing the words "Sugar-Free" in the individual item’s name. Selecting any of hem does bring up a customization page that also includes nutritional information listing the sugar content of each drink.
According to the website, both the 16-ounce Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha and Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte have 16 grams of sugar each. Moving up to the Venti sizes pushes the sugar amounts to 21 grams and 20 grams, respectively. For comparison, a single Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup from a standard 1.5-ounce two-pack contains 11 grams of sugar.
RELATED: Recall issued for over 122,000 cases of Gatorade sold in 37 states due to undeclared food colorings
"Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant," said Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of Hagens Berman, a Seattle-based law firm that specializes in class-action cases.
Starbucks pushed back on the lawsuit, claiming that the sugar in the beverages comes from the protein-boosted milk used to make them. The coffee chain explained that it does not add sugar to the drinks and the syrup that is added for flavoring is sugar-free.
"We believe these claims have no merit," a Starbucks spokesperson said Monday. "Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter."
The lawsuit is asking for damages on behalf of customers who bought the drinks believing they were sugar-free and for Starbucks to stop marketing them as "sugar-free."
The Source: Information for this article was taken from the Associated Press and Starbucks’ website. This story was reported from Orlando.

articles.title_orig: 2 People, Including Winter Haven High School Student, Killed in Florida Bus Crash
articles.title_zh: 2 People, Including Winter Haven High School Student, Killed in Florida Bus Crash
articles.content_orig:
Two people were killed after a major school bus crash in Winter Haven on Monday morning, according to the Polk County Sheriff's Office.
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said the incident happened around 6:15 a.m.
He said the school bus was traveling eastbound on Lucerne Park Road when a westbound white Chevy Malibu crashed into it.
Judd said the impact caused the bus to lose control and tear off a tire. The bus then collided head-on with a Jeep and ultimately overturned.
As a result, two people were killed, including a 10th-grade student.
In addition to the school bus, three other vehicles were involved in the crash.
The school bus was carrying 39 people, including 37 high school students, who were on their way to Winter Haven High School.
The other two people on the bus were identified as the school bus driver and the driver's 9-year-old daughter.
The Winter Haven Police Department said Lucerne Park Road was shut down in both directions at US-27. It has since reopened.
The Winter Haven Hospital confirmed it received 22 patients, including 19 pediatric patients and 3 adults.
The hospital said it has treated and released all patients except one pediatric patient who was transferred to another hospital.
Lakeland Regional Health confirmed it received 10 patients, including two who were transported by air and two taken in from other hospitals.
At around 3 p.m., the hospital said 7 patients have been treated and released and two patients remain under evaluation, with one expected to be released. One patient was admitted and remains in critical condition.
Polk County Public Schools confirmed the school bus involved in the crash did have seatbelts for students, adding that all of the school district's buses are equipped with lap belts.
"A PCPS school bus was involved in a serious accident this morning in Winter Haven, which claimed the life of a Winter Haven High student and another motorist.
This is devastating news for WHHS and our community. We are praying for the victims and their families. Thank you to the many dedicated first responders who provided essential support this morning."

The National Transportation Safety Board has opened an investigation into the crash in coordination with the sheriff's office.

articles.title_zh: What to know about a Russian lab worker's death and speculation about pneumonic plague
articles.content_orig:
A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.
The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.
The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.
Dozens quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.
Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.
The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.
Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.
Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.
The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles .
With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.
Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.
Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.
Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.
The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination , except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.
Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.
Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.
The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.
Evans, who wrote “ Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19 ,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”
Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”
WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.
People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.
There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.
“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”
For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.
Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.
In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

articles.title_orig: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
articles.title_zh: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
articles.content_orig:
President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters
Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%. That polling included the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip could prove dire for the Republican party a month ahead of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Before boarding a flight to Nebraska on Monday, Trump shrugged off questions about his approval ratings.
“I’m doing great,” Trump told a reporter, who’d asked about recent polls showing the president losing support among Latino voters, before blaming CNN and the media.
But according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll release Sunday, 59% of Latino voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, double the number that supported the party two years ago. According to that poll, just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance.
Trump has spent the past few days campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, despite even conservative states starting to show the loss of support. Some Republicans have also started to distance themselves from the president over issues like immigration as they attempt to hold onto local support.
With Americans souring on the economy, the war with Iran, and other key issues they attribute to the administration, the impact of the negative sentiments could reach far and wide.

articles.title_orig: Entergy Texas Names David Borde President and CEO
articles.title_zh: Entergy Texas Names David Borde President and CEO
articles.content_orig:
Electric utility company Entergy Texas has appointed a new president and CEO to head the company’s broader customer-centric strategies following the departure of former CEO Eliecer Viamontes.
On Monday, Entergy Texas announced that David Borde will now lead the company. The move comes as Viamontes departed for other opportunities, according to a company release.
Headshot of new president and CEO David Borde. | Credit: Entergy Texas
Prior to accepting the role as president and CEO, Borde, who joined Entergy in 2009, served as the company’s vice president of utility strategy and regulatory initiatives. In that role, he supported Entergy’s objectives by leading regulatory and tariff filing efforts while  providing ongoing strategic and regulatory counsel.
During his tenure, Borde held several other key leadership roles, including serving as director of corporate development based in Texas, vice president of investor relations and within the utility finance business partner organization.
The company noted that this regulatory focus has allowed the organization to keep pace with evolving customer needs.
“David has extensive experience in utility strategy, regulatory affairs and utility finance, along with his deep understanding of our business and customers,” said Drew Marsh, chair and CEO of Entergy. “He is a thoughtful and proven leader, and he will build on the strong foundation in Texas while advancing our commitment to providing safe, reliable and affordable energy to the communities we serve.”
Before joining Entergy, Borde worked in the investment banking division of Citigroup USA and as a lawyer at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. He earned a Juris Doctor degree from Duke University’s School of Law in 2001 and holds a business degree from the University of Paris.
