articles.title_orig: Midterm Election Updates: Democrats Target More GOP Strongholds as They Fight for Control of Congress
articles.title_zh: Midterm Election Updates: Democrats Target More GOP Strongholds as They Fight for Control of Congress
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four weeks out from Election Day, the Senate battleground map is growing after signs of improvement for Democrats in several red-leaning states.
For the first time this year, CNN’s list of 9 Senate seats most likely to flip expands to 10 to include Kansas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years . A new wave of polling also shows Democrats ahead or competitive in red states like Ohio, Alaska and Texas. All four states went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024.
To win the Senate majority, Democrats will need to pick up four Republican-held seats while defending three of their own, including Michigan.
Trump’s approval rating stands at 34%, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls, amid high frustration over the economy and the war he launched against Iran. Democrats have also seen surging enthusiasm in special elections since Trump returned to office and early signs of elevated turnout in early voting.
But they have also expressed unease over the massive amount of spending coming from the GOP. From the start of October through Election Day, Republicans are poised to outspend Democrats on advertising in eight of the ten most competitive Senate races, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, even though that advantage will be blunted by GOP-aligned outside groups having to spend more for ratings points than Democratic campaigns will.
Our ranking of the seats most likely to flip in November is based on CNN reporting, including conversations with strategists involved in Senate races, as well as our analysis of candidate fundraising, polling and the partisan environment in the states. The rankings are a snapshot of where the contests stand at this point and can shift as the midterm election season enters its final month.
North Carolina remains the state most likely to flip this year. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper, who has made affordability issues a centerpiece of his campaign, has a strong position over GOP nominee Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and Trump ally vying to replace Sen. Thom Tillis.
An Elon University/YouGov poll released last month showed Cooper up 11 points over Whatley among likely voters. The Senate Leadership Fund, a key Republican outside spending group, is pausing its ad campaign there. Over the weekend, Republican outside groups cut more than $15 million from their remaining ad bookings, according to AdImpact data.
Still, Trump campaigned with Whatley in North Carolina last month in an effort to turn out his base in a state he won three times.
Ohio moves up two spots on this list, a reflection of the prime position of former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Brown, who lost reelection to a fourth term by less than four points two years ago, has led GOP Sen. Jon Husted in most polls. A New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters conducted at the end of September showed a tight race, Brown at 49% and Husted at 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A Marist poll of registered voters in Ohio showed Brown up eight points over Husted last month.
In the NYT/Siena University poll, Husted’s favorability is at 37% while Brown is at 46%. That’s perhaps a reflection of Brown having a longer history with many Ohio voters than Husted, the former lieutenant governor appointed to take Vice President JD Vance’s seat last year.
Brown’s attacks on Husted over data centers – calling him “the face of data centers in Ohio” – have proven particularly potent as Republicans’ campaign arm in Washington has warned the issue is an “anchor” on Husted’s campaign.
Senate Democrats last week blocked a Husted-sponsored bill that would have recommended states take action on data center-related energy costs. And campaigning for Husted on Saturday, Trump defended data centers in southwestern Ohio, a reflection of the president’s longstanding opposition to pausing their construction.
In one buzzy digital spot released last week, Brown’s campaign also featured voters using expletives as they reacted to Husted’s past comments suggesting people living in poverty are “not very experienced at navigating the real world.” (Brown’s campaign is running an expletive-free version of the ad on TV.)
Republicans have pulled from a 2024 playbook to run ads attacking Brown on transgender politics, hoping that will move the needle in the state. Brown has responded with a TV spot of his own featuring voters talking about how Ohio already has laws addressing transgender policies and wanting candidates to focus on other issues.
One big question heading into the final stretch is whether GOP spending could help tighten this race. Republican groups are set to spend more than $80 million there from the start of October through Election Day while Democrats have allotted more than $50 million.
Alaska moves up two spots. The enormous and sparsely populated state is notoriously hard to poll, but a NYT/Siena poll of likely voters released Saturday found Democrat Mary Peltola up seven points over GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, 50 to 43%.
November’s contest will be determined by ranked-choice voting, and two others join Sen. Sullivan and Peltola on the ballot, including another GOP candidate named Dan Sullivan, a former schoolteacher. The possibility of voters confusing the same-name candidates has been a point of concern for Republicans ahead of November.
Democrats consider Peltola, a former congresswoman, as one of their strongest recruits, and she’s kept some national Democratic politicians like former Vice President Kamala Harris at arm’s length at a time when her opponent attempts to tie to her to “lower-48 liberals.”
Sullivan stood beside Trump in the Oval Office to tout a $54 billion investment from South Korea for the Alaska LNG pipeline project just weeks before the election. Peltola also moved quickly to praise the president’s announcement, saying she looks forward to “continuing this bipartisan work” with Trump.
Peltola’s demeanor towards aides and use of vulgar rhetoric came under scrutiny last month with a New York Times report detailing allegations of hostile behavior from some former aides. Her campaign denied any pattern of abusive pattern but acknowledged that Peltola has struggled at times to deal with the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, also came to her defense , noting Peltola’s personal struggles.
Maine drops two spots on our list. But the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson remains extremely competitive as the two prepare to debate for the first time this week.
A University of New Hampshire poll conducted last month found Jackson slightly ahead of Collins among Maine likely voters – 51% to 47% - marking the first public survey showing the Democrat with the advantage in the state. Other recent polls, including a CNN survey conducted by SSRS and a NYT/Siena poll , have shown no clear leader.
Collins remains in a vulnerable position given Harris won her state by 7 points in 2024. Polling has indicated the contest hinges more on negative views of the Maine senator and Trump than it does on perceptions about her Democratic opponent.
Democrats have hammered Collins for siding with Trump on consequential votes even as she’s struck out on her own on issues like tariffs and the Iran war. They have also seized on a ProPublica report alleging Collins’ office was involved in a pay-to-play scheme during her 2020 campaign. Collins has forcefully denied the allegations as a “political hit job.”
Collins has survived tough reelection battles in the past, and Republicans are leaning hard on reminding constituents of what she’s accomplished for the state. GOP groups also have spent millions on corruption ads of their own against Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, along with TV spots hammering the Democrat on tax policy .
Starting Tuesday, Collins and Jackson will have four debates over ten days.

articles.title_orig: DP World and Fundación Verde Profundo Advance Mangrove Restoration in the Dominican Republic
articles.title_zh: DP World and Fundación Verde Profundo Advance Mangrove Restoration in the Dominican Republic
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Partnership achieves 86% mangrove survival rate in Boca Chica and targets 1,000 planted seedlings by the end of 2026
NORTHAMPTON, MA / ACCESS Newswire / October 5, 2026 / DP World and Fundación Verde Profundo are expanding their mangrove restoration work in Boca Chica after achieving a 86% survival rate among more than 400 seedlings planted in the area's reef lagoon. The partnership now aims to reach 1,000 planted mangrove seedlings by the end of 2026.
Launched in 2025 , the partnership focuses on restoring coastal ecosystems near DP World's Caucedo terminal while strengthening biodiversity and the natural resilience of Boca Chica's coastline. The program includes ongoing monitoring and maintenance to support the long-term growth of restored mangroves.
Monitoring shows that approximately 48% of the planted mangroves have already developed aerial roots, an important sign of growth and adaptation. Mollusks, crustaceans, and juvenile fish have also been observed in restored areas, using the mangroves as shelter and nursery habitat.
The latest restoration activity on September 15 brought together 35 DP World employees and representatives from Fundación Verde Profundo for hands-on conservation work and education about the role mangroves play in protecting marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
"Economic development and environmental protection must advance together," said Manuel Martínez, CEO of DP World in the Dominican Republic . "Our two years of work with Fundación Verde Profundo show how strong partnerships can deliver measurable environmental results. We remain committed to supporting the recovery of coastal ecosystems and helping build healthier, more resilient communities".
Tasha Gough, CEO of Fundación Profundo, highlighted the progress achieved through this collaboration. "Mangrove restoration is a long-term process that requires technical monitoring, continuity, and collaboration among the public, private, and social sectors. One year after the first planting, the high survival rate of the seedlings and their continued development indicate that we are moving in a positive direction. Our goal is not simply to plant mangroves, but to support their establishment and assess how the ecosystem responds over time," she said.
Building a More Sustainable Logistics Hub
The mangrove program forms part of DP World's broader sustainability work in the Dominican Republic. In 2026, the company commissioned a 5,120-kW solar installation expected to reduce CO₂ emissions by more than 3,500 tons annually. DP World is also electrifying its terminal fleet , with now 41 fully electric internal transfer vehicles currently in operation at Caucedo.
The partnership with Fundación Verde Profundo also extends to environmental education. For example, during DP World's Global Volunteer Week , held in connection with the UN's International Volunteer Day, employees, customers, and community partners in the Dominican Republic take part in activities focused on mangrove conservation, biodiversity, and coastal resilience.
Together, these efforts reflect DP World's "Our World, Our Future" sustainability strategy and its approach to reducing the environmental impact of port operations while protecting the ecosystems surrounding them.
Learn more about sustainability in action at DP World in the Dominican Republic.

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_orig: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
articles.title_zh: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
articles.content_orig:
A new fact sheet released by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and the International Task Force on Teachers for Education 2030 examines the status of teachers, including how teachers are valued, supported and paid, 60 years after the adoption of the landmark 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers .
The fact sheet was released to mark World Teachers’ Day 2026 , bringing together ministers, teachers and education experts at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris to discuss how to strengthen the profession. Co-convened by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International, the celebration took place under the theme “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures”.
Every learner deserves a teacher who is well prepared, well supported and empowered to thrive in the profession. Realizing this right depends on how societies value teachers and the teaching profession. In fact, the value we place on teachers reflects the value we place on future generation.
How teachers are seen by society shapes whether they stay in their jobs. In 75% of the countries taking part in the OECD's TALIS 2024 survey , fewer than 40% of teachers felt that their profession was valued. Those who felt valued were over 10% less likely to think about leaving within five years.
The stakes are high: 58% of the teachers the world needs by 2030 will be hired not to expand the workforce, but to replace those who leave the profession. The fact sheet shows where the losses are greatest: attrition rates are 7.2% in pre-primary education, 5.4% in secondary and 4.7% in primary.
The new data also reveals that pre-primary and primary teachers earn slightly less than other professionals with similar qualifications. Overall, in two out of five of the 68 countries analyzed, teacher salaries remain below those of similarly qualified professionals across all education levels.
Teaching also comes with a heavy workload.  Teachers spend an average of 19 hours in the classroom per week, but work around 60 hours in total, much of it includes unpaid preparation, marking and administrative tasks. In primary schools, the global pupil-trained teacher ratio stands at 28 to 1, the highest of any level.
The fact sheet offers practical recommendations for governments and partners. These include giving teachers a seat at the table when policy is made, setting professional standards and career paths, offering competitive salaries and targeted incentives for hard-to-staff schools, making schools safer and more supportive, and cutting back unnecessary workload.
UNESCO works with countries to increase the supply of qualified, motivated teachers by improving policies relating to them and supporting quality training which meets learners’ needs. Special focus is placed on Africa, inclusion, gender sensitivity and digital technologies.
UNESCO and the ILO have also launched a joint revision of the 1966 Recommendation , guided by an Independent Expert Group through mid-2027.
As the work moves forward, the evidence is clear: attractive, respected and supported teaching professions are the foundation of quality education for every learner.
This article is related to the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals .

articles.title_orig: Googlebooks with Intel chipsets might have trouble with ‘complex’ Android apps
articles.title_zh: Googlebooks with Intel chipsets might have trouble with ‘complex’ Android apps
articles.content_orig:
According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps.
When Android apps made their debut on ChromeOS, one of the big downsides was that ARM-based machines ran those apps better than those using Intel chips. It was never a surprise given that Android apps are generally designed for devices running on an ARM architecture vs the x86 used on Intel chips.
Yet, the problem remains on Googlebook.
Despite the whole platform being Android-based this time around, Google confirmed in a statement to Android Authority that Intel-based Googlebook machines will still run into the occasional hiccup with “complex” Android apps and games, though the company emphasizes that “the vast majority” will work just fine.
The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box.
Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio.
I'm kind of surprised they even released Intel based models in the first place. From my understanding Googlebooks are more Android based than ChromeOS based and I don't know of any ARM based ChromeOS machines out there just like there are no x86 Intel based Android phones/tablets that I am aware of.
Also I suspect the Googlebooks using ARM based SoC's will probably edge out the Intel based ones in battery life.
Still, this is noteworthy as the first wave of Googlebook hardware includes mostly Intel-based machines. Laptops from Lenovo, Asus, and Acer all run on Panther Lake-generation Intel chips, while Dell and HP machines both use the Snapdragon X Elite (the 2024 chip, not the newer version).
Another chip used for Googlebook from MediaTek is also in the works, though no machines are using it just yet.
The first batch of Googlebook laptops are all available as of today.

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
articles.content_orig:
Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now. ”
Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”
Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro .
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo , and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups ,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

articles.title_orig: Trump plans executive order seeking to bring down high diesel costs
articles.title_zh: Trump plans executive order seeking to bring down high diesel costs
articles.content_orig:
The move would allow broader use of red dyed diesel, which carries no federal excise tax, but is not expected to boost overall supply
President Donald Trump is preparing to ease restrictions on the use of red dyed diesel, a tax-exempt variety of the fuel typically limited to off-road purposes, according to Bloomberg .
The administration is expected to announce the plan on Monday, according to Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources. Red dyed diesel is chemically identical to on-road diesel but is exempt from the 24-cents-per-gallon federal excise tax, so broadening its permitted use in on-road vehicles would effectively deliver a tax cut to drivers.
The measure is aimed at cutting costs for users of on-road vehicles such as pickup trucks, but would not directly lower expenses for farm equipment operators who already run on tax-exempt red diesel. It is also not expected to increase the overall supply of diesel, according to Bloomberg. Red diesel is drawn from the same national stockpile as conventional on-road fuel, and that stockpile is currently at a record seasonal low.
Retail diesel averaged $6.32 per gallon on Sunday, well off the all-time peak of $6.53 reached last month, yet nearly double the $3.76 a gallon that drivers paid on Feb. 28, the day the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins $ROL wrote on social media Monday that Trump "is taking action to deliver short-term relief for farmers and ranchers, including prioritizing diesel in the release of 100 million barrels of crude oil." Rollins separately told Fox Business that Trump would make an announcement on relief for farmers later Monday, without elaborating.
That move was preceded by a deal reached Friday in which Group of Seven nations and partner countries agreed to collectively release up to 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks, an outcome that followed sustained U.S. pressure on European allies.
Trump had previously floated banning U.S. diesel exports as a way to bring down domestic prices, a position that drew sharp opposition from industry groups including the American Petroleum Institute. Following the G7 agreement, Trump said he would not restrict foreign diesel sales. The administration has also pressured European nations including France and Germany to draw down their emergency petroleum reserves, with the U.S. at one point signaling the threat of an export ban if they refused to comply.
Monday's trip takes Trump to Grand Island, Nebraska, where the GOP is working to turn out farm-state voters before November's midterm elections.

articles.title_orig: Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf
articles.title_zh: Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Many white dwarfs accrete the debris of disrupted planetary bodies, detected in the form of metal enrichment in their atmospheres, dusty or gaseous circumstellar discs, and photometric transits from debris. The composition of accreted debris has been shown to be diverse yet overall closely resembles Solar System bodies. Here we report the discovery of a white dwarf accreting material that is unlike any Solar System object. The atmosphere of HS 0209+0832 is strongly enriched in trans-iron elements including zinc, copper and niobium but depleted in the canonical rock-forming elements silicon and iron. The composition of the accreted object is consistent with a candidate second-generation planet, formed from the stellar material ejected during the giant phase. The key abundance signature that differentiates it from a first-generation planet is the high enrichment of s-process elements. Photospheric helium and the absence of terrestrial rock-forming elements implies that the white dwarf is accreting from the escaped atmosphere of a photo-evaporating giant planet candidate. This is further supported by the detection of a sinusoidal photometric period of 4.399 ± 0.026 days at an amplitude of 0.120% ± 0.018%, which we attribute to thermal emission phase variability from a planetary day–night cycle or a transiting cometary tail of an evaporating gas giant. The discovery of this second-generation planet that is chemically distinct from first-generation material demonstrates that close-in planets around white dwarfs can form after the main sequence.
HS 0209+0832 is a hot, young white dwarf with an effective temperature of T eff ≈ 35,000 K, a cooling age of t cool ≈ 5 Myr and a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere with an ~1% trace of helium 1 . Such a mixed composition is unusual for a white dwarf of this temperature because helium should sink out of the atmosphere within months 2 , 3 . A far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum obtained in 1999 with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) onboard the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) revealed the presence of carbon, aluminium, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere 4 , as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified. Whereas the presence of helium and metals indicates ongoing accretion, the nature of that external source remained unexplained 4 .
In the 25 years since that study was published, the origin of photospheric metals detected in many other white dwarfs has been unambiguously confirmed as planetary debris 5 , 6 . This motivated a reanalysis of the observations of HS 0209+0832 obtained with HST/STIS, the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and the Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES) mounted on the Very Large Telescope (VLT), along with the broad-band photometry from Pan-STARRS and the Gaia parallax ( Methods ). In a first step, we determined T eff = 35,800 ± 500 K, a surface gravity of log g = 7.90 ± 0.02 and a helium abundance of log(He/H) = −1.90 ± 0.20 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Extended Data Table 1 ). With these parameters fixed, we computed extensive grids of synthetic white dwarf spectra 7 using detailed lists of metal transitions in the ultraviolet (Extended Data Table 2 ). We matched most of the previously unidentified lines to transitions of copper and niobium, with the latter identified using five Nb III lines and 57 Nb IV lines (Fig. 1 ). We carefully examined archival FUSE 8 spectra of 33 known metal-enriched white dwarfs with temperatures 20,000 K < T eff < 77,000 K and confirm non-detections for niobium within that sample.
The FUSE and HST spectra (both black) of HS 0209+0832 contain many lines of C, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb as well as strong hydrogen and helium lines. The unusual structure of the He II line is not well reproduced by the model, which could be caused by additional absorption from circumstellar gas. We show the model fit used to obtain metal abundances in red.
We measured the photospheric abundances ( Methods ) for nine metals and calculated upper limits on 15 metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). We excluded any lines originating from the interstellar medium in our fit (Extended Data Table 4 ). At the temperature of HS 0209+0832, radiative levitation can support certain elements against gravitational diffusion. We investigated this effect for all detected elements, as well as for N, P and S for which we determined upper limits ( Methods ). We selected these volatiles because they are commonly detected in hot white dwarfs 8 , 9 ; thus, it is unusual they are not observed in HS 0209+0832. We find that, for the measured abundances, radiative levitation is negligible for Ca, S, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb. Assuming a steady state between accretion into and diffusion out of the white dwarf atmosphere, we computed the diffusion fluxes for each element. We adopt these mass fluxes as being representative of the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832, as they correct the photospheric abundances for the differential sinking timescales of individual metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). By contrast, the abundances of C, N, Al, Si and P are subject to radiative support. These elements must still have an external origin 10 , 11 , but our analysis cannot determine their mass fractions within the accreting material.
We compare the abundances of the parent body accreting onto HS 0209+0832 to the entire sample of white dwarfs accreting rocky material 12 and to Solar System meteorites 13 , but find no compositional matches (Fig. 2 ). Whereas silicon and iron are two major components of planetary bodies in the inner Solar System, with a combined mass fraction of ~48% in the bulk Earth 14 , we detect only traces of silicon in the atmosphere of HS 0209+0832, compatible with the support provided by radiative levitation, and no iron. By contrast, the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 is rich in nickel, which shares many geochemical properties with iron, and we measure a nickel-to-iron ratio of Ni/Fe > 2.09, compared with ~0.05 within CI chondrites 15 and the bulk Earth 14 . We find that the trans-iron elements are strongly enhanced relative to calcium compared with solar abundances, particularly niobium, which is over three orders of magnitude more abundant than in the Sun.
We show the number abundances of the metals (Z) in the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 (red stars) with respect to calcium, normalized to bulk Earth (BE) 74 (solid black line) for all detected metals and metals with strict upper limits. The error bars represent 1 σ uncertainties, and the arrows represent upper limits. The dashed red lines represent the predicted abundance from radiative levitation alone. For comparison, we include the solar abundance pattern 75 (dashed black line), comet Halley 76 (black points) and the abundances of several white dwarfs accreting bulk Earth-like 5 , core-rich 77 , mantle-rich 78 and icy 16 material (green, blue, brown and purple points, respectively).
Most enriched white dwarfs are depleted in volatile elements such as C, N and S, but a minority are volatile enriched, which can be due to accreting either icy bodies 16 or the atmosphere of a giant planet 17 . The only volatile detected in HS 0209+0832 is carbon (Extended Data Fig. 2 ), with a high photospheric abundance that is compatible with fiducial predictions from radiative levitation. However, there are both theoretical and empirical reasons to believe that our fiducial radiative levitation predictions overestimate the importance of this effect. articles.title_orig: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.title_zh: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.content_orig:
In a cosmic first, scientists say they have detected a planet that may have formed from the burned remains of its dead host star.
The planet is likely a gas giant orbiting a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832 located about 270 light-years from Earth , according to the authors of a study published Monday in the journal Nature Astronomy. After analyzing observations from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and other instruments, the team found chemical evidence that suggests the planet could have condensed from material expelled by the star as it fizzled out of energy and collapsed into a white dwarf.
When a sunlike star dies, it first rapidly expands into a red giant and then sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a much smaller but dense, hot core — known as a white dwarf. Some of the first-generation planets, those that originally formed at the same time as the star, can survive this cataclysmic event if their orbit is wide enough. Astronomers have observed a handful of such first-generation survivors revolving around white dwarfs, but never before have they recorded a so-called second-generation planet — an entirely new world made from a dead star’s debris.
Planet found orbiting a dead star could preview what will happen to our solar system
The telltale sign that HS 0209+0832 might have birthed a new planet is unusual traces of heavy elements on the white dwarf’s surface that the study authors believe is planetary material raining down onto the leftover core. “This planetary material is very rich in an element called niobium,” said lead study author Jamie Williams, a doctoral student in the department of physics of the University of Warwick in England. “It’s the first time that this element is found in a white dwarf, and this implies that the planetary material is made from the ashes of the star as it died.”
Further analysis of observations from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite or TESS revealed a faint brightness signal repeating every 4.4 days — evidence that the researchers say is consistent with a giant planet orbiting the white dwarf.
“What’s interesting about planets orbiting close to white dwarfs is that because white dwarfs cool over time, their habitable zone is very stable. A second-generation planet could form and then be in the habitable zone for tens of billions of years,” Williams said.
Such a large period of stability could provide more ideal conditions for life, but more work is required to validate the second-generation planet discovery, he added. “It’s not a confirmed planet,” Williams said. “It’s only a candidate for now.”
After the red giant phase when a dying star quickly puffs up, it becomes a nuclear furnace that can produce various elements. However, once that fuel runs out and the star transforms into a white dwarf, the heavy elements — including nobium — sink downward rapidly, leaving only lighter elements such as hydrogen and helium on the surface. The researchers determined that the niobium detected on HS 0209+0832 must therefore come from the star’s surroundings. “We think these elements fell onto the white dwarf’s surface because the white dwarf is very hot and emitting loads of extreme ultraviolet radiation, which is stripping the atmosphere of a nearby planet,” Williams said.
The idea of second-generation planets has existed for at least as long as astronomers have known about exoplanets, said study coauthor David J. Wilson, a research associate at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder.
Scientists detected the very first exoplanets around a pulsar — a type of rapidly rotating dead star — and because pulsars form as a result of massive explosions called supernovas, these planets are likely second-generation, as any original planets would have been destroyed by the immense blast, Wilson explained.
“Although white dwarfs don’t form via supernova, they are surrounded by debris,” he said via email. “You have the planets that were lucky enough to survive the star’s giant phases, the shattered remains of those that weren’t, and leftover gas and dust ejected by the star as it turned from a giant to a white dwarf. So it’s a compelling idea that all that stuff might coalesce into new planets.”
Astronomers still don’t know all the details about how first-generation planets form, which means the potential mechanisms behind this newly reported second-generation planet are even more uncertain. The planet-forming process might have derived from a collision between the dying star and a second celestial body, according to Williams. “There could have been another object close to the core of the star, maybe a star around 20% the mass of the sun, or a brown dwarf,” said Williams, referring to a class of cool objects that are an intermediate between a star and a planet.
If a second object fell into the star during its giant phase, it could have prevented all the dust and gas from spreading out into a massive cloud, making some of it spin in a disk. This disk would then have continued to rotate around the white dwarf, birthing a planet. “In a regular white dwarf there’s no disc, because the star’s material will just be ejected outwards during the red giant phase,” Williams added.
Astronomers discover never-before-seen two-faced star
The researchers plan to use Hubble and NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to observe the system again over the next year, but they also requested time with the more powerful James Webb Space Telescope, which could provide more clues about the existence or features of the planet.
If confirmed, this distant world would belong to an entirely new planetary class and suggest that more second-generation planets could exist around white dwarfs, Williams said.
The discovery would also have implications for our own cosmic neighborhood, Wilson said. “The sun will eventually become a white dwarf, so we’re also looking at the future of the solar system here — maybe the Sun will get a new planet someday!”
The new discovery of a potential second-generation planet is incredibly exciting, said Sarah Casewell, a lecturer at the School of Physics and Astronomy of the University of Leicester, England, who was not involved with the study.
“We know of a large number of white dwarfs that are polluted by planetary material which is similar in composition to rocks within our solar system,” she wrote in an email. “However, in this case, the white dwarf is polluted by incredibly unusual material and the composition of this material is similar to atoms we see being created as stars end their lives.”
More than 95% of all stars in the universe will eventually become white dwarfs, and astronomers have already cataloged hundreds of thousands of them. Finding a planet that has formed after the white dwarf would mean that second-generation planets around other white dwarfs are possible — and that after our sun dies, new planets could emerge in our own solar system, Casewell said.
Radio signal detected for the first time from a planet outside our solar system
Previous observations of white dwarfs have shown that some planetary systems survive a star’s self-destruction, but the recent findings open the possibility of the genesis of new planets, said Amy Bonsor, an associate professor at the University of Cambridge in England, who also did not participate in the work. “This paradigm shift allows us to consider whether in the future we could characterise or investigate the potential habitability of these second-generation planetary systems,” she wrote in an email.
This discovery would also add more evidence to research that has shown planetary systems are varied and complex, even after the host star dies, according to Susan Mullally, a mission scientist at the Space Telescope Science Institute, the science operations center for Hubble.

articles.title_orig: A tropical system is likely in the Gulf this week despite El Niño. Here are the latest scenarios
articles.title_zh: A tropical system is likely in the Gulf this week despite El Niño. Here are the latest scenarios
articles.content_orig:
A tropical depression or storm has a high chance to form in the Gulf this week and breathe life into the tail end of an Atlantic hurricane season squashed by El Niño .
Get live updates and alerts. Download the CNN Weather app.
The Gulf is often a hot bed for late-season storms. Right on cue, chances are increasing for an area of stormy weather festering in the Gulf’s Bay of Campeche to spin up into one by midweek, according to the National Hurricane Center.
The next storm name in the Atlantic is Isaias (ees-ah-EE-ahs).
Exactly where the storm could track or how strong it could get is still up in the air.
Gulf water is record warm for this time of year, primed to generate and help strengthen any system. But this potential storm’s overall strength could be capped by less favorable conditions in the atmosphere.
No matter its final fate, heavy rain is a concern on the Gulf Coast and in other parts of the South by late this week.
All three scenarios are still possible, but it’s looking more likely that a tropical system will form for at least some period of time.
As this year has already shown, it doesn’t take a hurricane-strength system to cause significant impacts, particularly in a warming world that’s making tropical systems wetter.
Tropical storms Arthur and Edouard didn’t last long, but their heavy rain resulted in significant flash flooding and water rescues. Parts of Louisiana and Mississippi took the brunt of Arthur’s flooding while Edouard dropped over 20 inches of rain in eastern Texas.
Parts of Alabama, Georgia, the Florida Panhandle, southeast Louisiana and Mississippi are most at risk of heavy rain from this system. The downpours could start to ramp up along the coast as soon as Friday and then continue to soak the region while creeping farther inland through the weekend.
Several inches of rain could fall, but it’s too soon to pinpoint which locations might see the most and could experience flash flooding.
Four named storms — that’s tropical storm strength or greater — typically form in October and November, but some hurricane seasons can have a stronger finish while others quiet down.
The last few years illustrate this year-to-year ebb and flow. Seven storms formed during October and November in 2024, but just two formed during the same time in 2023.
Late-season storms tend to form closer to the United States, including in the Gulf, Caribbean and off the Southeast coast, which makes them more likely to impact land.
While there are usually fewer storms, they can still be destructive.
Last year, Category 5 Hurricane Melissa devastated Jamaica in October’s final week.
Hurricane Michael roared into the Florida Panhandle on October 10, 2018, becoming the latest landfalling Category 5 on record in the US. And Hurricane Sandy may be the most notorious of all: It morphed into a hybrid superstorm in late-October 2012 and walloped the East Coast.
Super El Niño’s grip on the Atlantic basin means a repeat of notorious late-season hurricanes is less likely this year. Its storm-killing wind is the main reason this season could go hurricane-free for the first time in reliable records .

articles.title_zh: Spain's gambler PM Sanchez seeks to defy the odds again on a snap election
articles.content_orig:
Spanish PM Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election days after Congress voted against measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis
SÃ¡nchez's government had presented the measures in response to nationwide protests, triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home for failing to pay a sharp rent increase
The woman's rent was raised from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since 2018. Spain was not due to hold a general election until summer 2027 - here's what happened last time
Most polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election, which will take place on 29 November
SÃ¡nchez clearly wants to take the initiative - but it's going to be very tough for him to remain in power, writes Guy Hedgecoe in Madrid
Edited by Rorey Bosotti and Imogen James
Dan Woodland Live reporter
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election on 29 November, bringing forward the vote which was originally scheduled for the summer of 2027.
The move follows weeks of protests across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants, sparked last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid following a sharp rent increase.
SÃ¡nchezâs leftist coalition government failed to pass emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis on Friday - but is now expected to approve measures on Tuesday.
The premier's position has also been marred by multiple corruption investigations in recent months involving former members of government and even his wife and brother.
Opposition parties welcomed the snap election, with the leader of the conservative People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o declaring Spain will "at last" say "what it thinks", and leader of the far-right Spanish party Vox Santiago Abascal saying he was "glad" about the announcement.
Meanwhile, members of SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians expressed confidence that they would be re-elected and the prime minister would "pull off a comeback".
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next vote, however they would be expected to need Vox's support to form a government.
This will be SÃ¡nchez's sixth election in 11 years, and if he is to remain in power, he needs to upset some tough odds, writes our reporter in Madrid .
We're ending our live coverage here, but you can read more in our news story .
With eight years in power, Pedro SÃ¡nchez is now Spain's second longest-serving prime minister in recent history.
His political career has been marked by dramatic twists and turns, including his resignation as Socialist Party leader in 2016 after losing the support of senior party figures. Just seven months later, he staged a remarkable comeback, returning to the leadership with the backing of grassroots members.
SÃ¡nchez has called an early election despite opinion polls suggesting he may struggle to secure enough support to remain in power.
Some analysts believe that focusing the campaign on Spain's housing crisis could help mobilise left-wing voters and steer the debate away from other challenges facing the government, including the situation in Ceuta and corruption allegations involving figures close to SÃ¡nchez.
It is not the first time SÃ¡nchez has taken a major political gamble. In 2023, he called a snap election after his party suffered heavy losses in regional and local elections.
Polls at the time also suggested he was heading for defeat.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, SÃ¡nchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to stay in office, thanks to agreements with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Opposition parties accused him of "selling out Spain" in order to remain in power.
The High Court of Justice of Madrid has rejected a request to disperse an encampment in Puerto Del Sol in the Spanish capital.
Protesters have set up tents in the famous square since 27 September, court documents show.
The court rejected the Community of Madrid's request for police to clear the square on Monday. A new hearing is expected to take place on Wednesday.
A trade union has also called on people to continue protesting in the street against issues with wages and housing ahead of the snap election.
The general secretary of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) trade union confederation, Unai Sordo, says: "We must continue with a path of mobilisation, of street protests as we had announced, regarding wages and housing measures, and that will be our course in the coming months."
People in the streets of Madrid say they welcome news of the snap election called by Prime Minister SÃ¡nchez this morning.
âI think itâs good given the situation thatâs arisen", Raomon Diaz tells Reuters.
"Young people have been given little prospect for the future. And Iâd like to see a truly left-wing government finally come to power.â
Protester Florencio Diaz described the election announcement as a "great victory for the protests in the streets".
Florencio Diaz says Spanish people are struggling with the cost of living
"Weâre in a very difficult situation, with the cost of living rising and, above all, the abuse taking place in the housing market", he says.
However, Sandra - who is also protesting against Spain's housing crisis - expressed reservations about what the future holds.
âTo be honest, Iâm a bit worried about what might happen. But itâs certainly true that with the government we have, things arenât moving forward.â
Sandra says she's worried about Spain's future
The Spanish government is expected to approve measures on Tuesday aimed at tackling the housing crisis that parliament rejected last week .
The measures include a suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030 and an automatic renewal of rental contracts.
The government failed to pass them last week, after they were opposed by the People's Party (PP), Vox, and Junts.
Once the government approves the measures, SÃ¡nchez has 30 days to get them ratified. But the Madrid-based political newspaper Moncloa suggests that the prime minister's calling of a snap election could help him do this without congress, as parliament will be dissolved before those 30 days are up.
When congress isn't sitting, ratifying the measures falls to a committee which has a more favourable political make-up for SÃ¡nchez and doesn't require support from the Junts party, the newspaper says.
The deputy prime minister of Spain Yolanda DÃ­az has called for rent caps and a shortened workday
Members of Pedro SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians have continued to react to the Spanish snap election.
The deputy prime minister of Spain, Yolanda DÃ­az - who is part of the Sumar movement - says in a post on Bluesky: "We are going to win again."
DÃ­az says the group will cap rents, shorten the workday and raise the minimum wage.
Health minister MÃ³nica GarcÃ­a says in a post on X that the "Spanish people will rise to the occasion and prevail over the resentment of international hate".
Meanwhile Justice minister FÃ©lix BolaÃ±os says on X that the prime minister "will pull off a comeback" and leave the People's Party and Vox "without a government".
Catalan President Salvador Illa Roca says elections will be a "moment to decide between continuing to advance or going backwards". "Catalonia will stand with Pedro SÃ¡nchez," he adds.
SÃ¡nchez celebrates beside his wife Begona Gomez, after winning the general elections in 2019
These will be the sixth elections that Pedro SÃ¡nchez has contested as Socialist leader since 2015.
He has only won two of those - the 2019 ballot which was repeated after being inconclusive - and yet he has been in power since winning a no-confidence motion against his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy, in 2018.

articles.title_orig: More than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries may get one-time $90 payment — here's who qualifies
articles.title_zh: More than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries may get one-time $90 payment — here's who qualifies
articles.content_orig:
More than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries may soon receive a one-time $90 payment from the federal government to offset their Medicare Part B premiums, the White House announced Friday.
President Donald Trump said Friday on Truth Social that his administration will start sending the payments "immediately."
Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary and preventative services, currently has around 62.9 million enrollees, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
About 20.8 million Medicare Part B enrollees will be eligible for the direct payments, according to CMS.
The one-time $90 payment isn't a significant offset for those consumers: For 2026, the standard Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 per month, which works out to about $2,434.80 for the calendar year.
Most eligible seniors will receive a $90 direct deposit payment in early October, according to a White House fact sheet. The payments are separate from the $500 refund checks the administration is sending to Obamacare enrollees.
Most eligible beneficiaries will receive a direct deposit on or around Oct. 8, according to a fact sheet from CMS. Qualifying seniors without direct deposit will receive a check at their mailing address on file with Medicare. Those checks will be sent later in October, according to CMS.
Medicare Part B enrollees who do not qualify include people who get premium assistance from Medicaid and those who pay income-related monthly adjustment amounts — an extra surcharge, also known as IRMAAs , added to monthly premiums for individuals with incomes that exceed certain amounts. Beneficiaries who do not live in the U.S. or who are enrolled in Medicare Advantage are not eligible, either.
The $90 payments will come from unutilized funds in the Medicare Improvement Fund, according to the White House, which has $2 billion authorized by Congress for improvements to Medicare's fee-for-service program.
To check eligibility for the $90 payment, the White House recommends seniors call Medicare at 1-800-633-4227. Beneficiaries may check on their payment status by calling the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213, beginning on Oct. 15.
In 2027, the standard Medicare Part B premium is estimated to increase to $209.50 per month, according to a June report from Medicare's trustees. That's $6.60 more per month than what beneficiaries currently pay, or a $79.20 increase for the year.
Medicare Part B premiums are typically deducted directly from monthly Social Security benefits. As a result, Medicare Part B premium payments affect the increase Social Security beneficiaries see from the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to be announced by the Social Security Administration this month. Experts estimate the annual increase may range from 3.5% to 3.6% based on government inflation data, which would be the highest increase in three years.

﻿The RAMpocalypse’s next victim is a seven year old streaming box.
Nvidia’s Shield TV streaming boxes are the latest victims of the memory shortage that has seen prices increase dramatically for everything from digital cameras to game consoles . When the Shield TV Pro launched nearly seven years ago with an upgraded Tegra X1+ processor, 3GB of RAM, and 16GB of storage, it sold for $199.99. But starting on October 2nd Nvidia increased its price by $100 to $299.99 as a result of the increased cost of components, according to Ars Technica .
When the Pro model was first announced in 2019 Nvidia also debuted an updated entry-level version of the Shield TV with the same processor but 2GB of RAM and 8GB of storage priced at $149.99. Unfortunately, it will no longer be an option for those now looking for a cheaper alternative to the Shield TV Pro. Nvidia has stopped production of the standard Shield TV model and moving forward it’s focusing its efforts on only manufacturing the Pro option, according to Gizmodo .
High demand for Nvidia’s other hardware including GPUs and AI chips has been a major contributor to the dramatic price increases of components and devices over the past few years. So while this price increase may reduce demand for the Shield TV Pro while competing streaming boxes like the $149 Google TV Streamer are much cheaper (even after recent price hikes ), it won’t affect Nvidia’s value as the company continues to dominate the AI race.

articles.title_orig: iCloud+ just rolled out an improved perk for subscribers
articles.title_zh: iCloud+ just rolled out an improved perk for subscribers
articles.content_orig:
iCloud+ includes a lot more than additional storage, and one of the service’s perks for subscribers—custom email domains—just got even better.
When creating a new email account, you can always go with a standard @gmail.com or @icloud.com domain. But there’s also a more personalized option.
Third-party services offer custom email addresses at a monthly cost. But unbeknownst to many, iCloud+ lets you create custom email addresses at no extra cost when you own the domain.
With iCloud+, you can set up email addresses that end in something personal to you or your business. It’s one of the service’s most underrated perks, and it just got better.
As detailed by pdfu on X , Apple has now increased the number of email addresses you can create per custom domain.
iCloud+ now lets you use up to 10 personalized email addresses per custom domain.
Previously, you were limited to just 3 personalized addresses per domain. The higher limit of 10 addresses is a big expansion that business owners in particular should appreciate. I’ve also seen plenty of families set up custom domains for their family members, and the higher limit will come in handy for that use case too.
Custom email domains with iCloud+ are available for all subscribers, and you can learn how to set them up here .
Do you use custom email addresses with your iCloud+ subscription? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.title_zh: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.content_orig:
The day before Cabrini Day, Archbishop James Golka made his first official visit to Mother Cabrini Shrine, celebrating a saint whose courage, compassion and missionary faith still challenge Catholics today.
There are certain days at Mother Cabrini Shrine when the past and present seem to come together in a particularly meaningful way. This Cabrini Day is one of them.
As Mother Cabrini Shrine celebrated Colorado’s Frances Xavier Cabrini Day, the Shrine also welcomed Archbishop James Golka for his first official visit — a fitting occasion for the new Archbishop of Denver to visit the holy ground dedicated to a woman whose faith, courage and missionary spirit left such a lasting mark on Colorado.
For Mother Cabrini Shrine, Cabrini Day is much more than a date on the calendar. It is an opportunity to remember the remarkable woman who first came to Denver in 1902 and whose footsteps eventually led her into the foothills west of the city. It was here that Mother Cabrini walked, prayed and cared for the girls from the Queen of Heaven Orphanage. More than a century later, pilgrims continue to come to this same holy ground seeking prayer, peace, healing and a deeper encounter with God.
In 2020, Colorado established Frances Xavier Cabrini Day as a state holiday, observed on the first Monday in October. It became the first paid state holiday in the nation named in honor of a woman — a remarkable distinction and a recognition of the impact Mother Cabrini’s life and work had on Colorado.
But the significance of Cabrini Day extends beyond remembering what Mother Cabrini accomplished more than a century ago. Her life continues to offer an example for the Church and the world today.
Mother Cabrini was a woman of extraordinary faith, but she was also a woman of action. She saw a need and responded. She crossed oceans, overcame obstacles and went wherever she believed God was calling her. Again and again, she said yes — to God, to those who needed her and to the mission placed before her.
(Photo by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
That message was echoed by Archbishop Golka during his homily at the 11:00 a.m. Mass.
Reflecting on Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life and witness, he said: “If the world had 100 more Mother Cabrinis, the faith and the Church would grow in ways that could hardly be imagined.”
He described Mother Cabrini as a woman who had the heart of a mother, caring deeply for those in need and offering an incredible example of faith lived through service. He also spoke about the importance of seeking the intercession of Mother Cabrini and all the saints, expressing his hope that pilgrims who come to the Shrine experience her intercession in their own lives and emphasizing that her witness remains as important today as it was during her lifetime.
That relevance was especially evident as the archbishop referenced “A Pilgrim People, A Shared Home,” an interfaith letter released in conjunction with Cabrini Day, affirming the dignity of every human life, with particular attention to migrant brothers and sisters. The message carries special significance on a day honoring Mother Cabrini, the patron saint of immigrants, whose ministry was shaped by her determination to accompany immigrants and others who found themselves vulnerable or in need.
More than a century later, the circumstances may be different, but Mother Cabrini’s example continues to call people to recognize the dignity of those around them and to respond with compassion.
After Mass, Mother Cabrini Shrine hosted a Festival of Nations that featured traditional music, dance and food from around the world. (Photos by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
Following Mass, Archbishop Golka greeted the faithful before joining the Shrine community for the Festival of Nations. The celebration was filled with joy and color, with foods representing cultures from around the world, people dressed in traditional clothing, and music and dance, including traditional Matachines dancing.
The celebration of nations is especially fitting on Cabrini Day. Mother Cabrini’s own life crossed borders, cultures and languages, and her mission was rooted in welcoming and caring for people far from home. More than a century later, the many cultures gathered together at the Shrine offered a beautiful reflection of both the universality of the Church and the mission she began.
Archbishop Golka’s first official visit was also a reminder that Mother Cabrini Shrine remains very much alive. Her mission continues through the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the clergy who serve the Shrine, its staff and volunteers, and the countless pilgrims who make their way to this holy ground each year. The life and ministry of a place like Mother Cabrini Shrine are sustained by many hands, many hearts and a shared commitment to carrying the mission forward.
Cabrini Day offers an opportunity not only to celebrate Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life, but also to consider what her example asks of all of us today.
Mother Cabrini saw those who were struggling and moved toward them. She trusted deeply in the Heart of Jesus, relied on prayer and refused to let seemingly insurmountable obstacles keep her from the work God had placed before her.
As Archbishop Golka reminded those gathered at the Shrine, the Church still needs Mother Cabrini. And perhaps one of the greatest ways to honor her is to continue the mission she so courageously began.
For those who have never visited Mother Cabrini Shrine — or perhaps have not been in many years — Cabrini Day offers a wonderful invitation to come and discover the woman behind the name. Walk where she walked, pray where she prayed, learn her story and discover why, more than a century later, St. Frances Xavier Cabrini and her mission still have so much to say to the world today.
Colorado Catholic Conference

A weekend comment about a Texas chip venture is testing the most visible outside endorsement of Intel 's ( NASDAQ:INTC ) foundry turnaround. Intel stock is at $114.52, down 4% in morning trading, carrying a loss the rest of the chip group isn't sharing. At issue is whether Intel keeps its singular role at one of the most closely followed chip projects in the U.S.
The selling pressure is barely reaching Advanced Micro Devices ( NASDAQ:AMD ) and NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ). AMD stock is at $628.89, down 0.8%, while NVIDIA stock is up 0.5%.
For a read on the wider sector, the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( NASDAQ:SOXX ) is down 0.7%, and the Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) is down 0.2%. The move in Intel stock is its own.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( NYSE:TSM ), the world's largest dedicated contract chipmaker, is central to the weekend news. Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla ( NASDAQ:TSLA ), confirmed that discussions between Taiwan Semiconductor and Terafab, his Texas chip venture, are under way, describing them as "Just discussions, but something may come of it." Intel joined Terafab in April as the venture's sole named manufacturing partner, with Intel's next-generation chipmaking technology designated as the facility's only identified process.

Terafab's planned output is reserved for Musk's own companies, which made Intel's role there a showcase for its manufacturing ambitions and a signal to other potential foundry customers, and a Taiwan Semiconductor role would place an established contract manufacturer alongside Intel at the project Intel backed first. That shift carries weight because Intel's external foundry revenue came to just $293 million in the second quarter of 2026, leaving few outside wins as visible as Terafab.
Susquehanna added a second concern, stating that Intel has likely continued to lose central processing unit (CPU) share in laptops and desktops during the third quarter of 2026, with AMD gaining ground. Those sections sit inside Intel's Client Computing Group, which generated $8.88 billion in revenue in the second quarter.
Intel's bull case rests on Terafab being one project inside a wider foundry turnaround that has already lifted Intel stock sharply higher this year, and Musk's own words frame the talks as early. Output on Intel's 18A node ran 25% above target in the second quarter, and Intel Foundry revenue reached $5.8 billion. On the July earnings call, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated that he is "more confident than ever of the strategic significance and unique value proposition of Intel foundry."
The bear case holds that Intel's seat at Terafab served as its most visible outside validation. Adding Taiwan Semiconductor would reduce that standing just as Susquehanna describes share losses in Intel's core processor business. Losses at Intel Foundry still reached $2.1 billion in the second quarter, and Intel stock trades at 63x forward earnings, which leaves little room if either concern deepens.
Management stated on the second-quarter call that version 0.9 of its Intel 14A process design kit was on track for October, a milestone Intel tied to growing external customer interest. Any formal Terafab agreement with Taiwan Semiconductor could change how the market values Intel's position at the project.
Intel's turnaround is showing measurable progress. The progress is in yields, output and foundry revenue, though Terafab now looks like a shared proof point, and a premium forward multiple leaves investors little room if Taiwan Semiconductor's role grows.

articles.title_orig: When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights for the best deals, according to Google
articles.title_zh: When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights for the best deals, according to Google
articles.content_orig:
In trying to score the cheapest airfares for the holidays, when you book a flight often matters just as much as your travel dates. And this year, booking early is particularly important as airfares creep higher, new Google data shows.
Flights for travel around Thanksgiving will be cheapest in October, while people traveling around Christmas should lock in their itineraries by around Halloween, according to Google Flights.
It's best to book as early as possible when your travel dates are relatively fixed. For Thanksgiving, consumers will find the lowest fares 34 days before departure, according to Google Flights, which based its findings on five years of flight data. Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, making Oct. 22 the best day to book travel for the Wednesday before the holiday. For the lowest fares on Turkey Day trips, travelers should aim to purchase tickets between 57 and 21 days before departure.
For flights around Christmas, the lowest fares will be available 56 days before departure. Travelers can land better deals between 33 and 67 days before their trips, according to Google Flights (as of Oct. 5, there are roughly 80 days before Christmas). The best flight deals will emerge between late October and mid-November, according to Google.
To save money on flights, experts also recommend traveling off-peak, when fewer people will swarm the nation's airports. Data from the fare aggregator Hopper shows that traveling on Monday or Tuesday before Thanksgiving, rather than on Wednesday, can yield savings. Avoid returning on Sunday, Nov. 29, the company said.
The same advice applies around Christmas. Hopper advises avoiding flying on Dec. 18, 19 and 20 and on Dec. 27, the Sunday after Christmas Day.
Americans should expect higher-than-usual flight prices due to the Iran war, which has raised oil and jet fuel prices, the largest expense for airlines after personnel. Before the Middle East conflict began in late February, jet fuel averaged $99 per barrel globally, according to the International Air Transport Association. It peaked at $209 in April and hit $195 a barrel in mid-September, IATA said, citing data from S&P Global Energy Platts.
Hopper data shows that domestic round-trip airfares for Thanksgiving are averaging $402, up 31% from last year. Domestic round-trip Christmas flights are averaging $452, up 23%  from last year.
