articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Nebraska to rescue GOP seat as his beef import plan angers rural voters
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Nebraska to rescue GOP seat as his beef import plan angers rural voters
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is taking his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska on Monday, campaigning alongside GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats .
Trump is headed to Grand Island, Nebraska, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama . On Wednesday, he’ll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
“The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill.
Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now he is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.
Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy , including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It’s a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close. But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha , considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats.
Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November.
Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments.
With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Navy and Air Force veteran Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch.
Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee earlier this year, but Burbank specifically campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general elections in November, and she has since formally dropped out of the race.
Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents.
Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023.

articles.title_zh: Old World Christmas Turns the Holiday Favorite Royal Dansk® Cookie Tin Into a Glass Ornament
articles.content_orig:
SPOKANE, Wash., Oct. 5, 2026
Old World Christmas has partnered with Royal Dansk ® to turn the Danish butter cookie tin into a hand-painted glass ornament, arriving just in time for the 2026 holiday season.
SPOKANE, Wash. , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For 60 years, the Royal Dansk® blue tin has been part of holiday traditions around the world. First filled with Danish Butter Cookies, it often takes a second life storing buttons, thread, and family keepsakes. Now, that beloved blue tin has been reimagined. Old World Christmas , the premier brand of hand-crafted glass ornaments, has partnered with Royal Dansk to turn its iconic Danish Butter Cookie tin into a mouth-blown, hand-painted glass ornament. The Butter Cookies Tin Ornament is available this holiday season at OldWorldChristmas.com .
Why this partnership matters Few cookies are as recognizable as the iconic Royal Dansk blue tin. Often repurposed to hold sewing supplies and treasured mementos, the tin has earned a lasting place in homes for generations. That's the nostalgia and tradition this ornament celebrates.
Old World Christmas has spent more than 45 years turning everyday objects and cultural touchstones into collectible keepsakes. Pairing that craft with one of the most recognizable tins in the world gives shoppers a way to keep the memory out year-round, not just for the few weeks the cookies last.
"The Royal Dansk tin is already in millions of homes. We just made a version you can hang on the tree," said Neal Applefeld, President and CEO of Old World Christmas. "We love taking the everyday objects and traditions people recognize and turning them into keepsakes they can enjoy year after year."
"For generations, the Royal Dansk blue tin has been a cherished holiday tradition," said Kris Nance, Brand Manager at Royal Dansk. "We've heard countless stories about families sharing our butter cookies and then finding new uses for the tin long after the cookies were gone. Seeing this iconic symbol reimagined as a holiday ornament is a wonderful way to celebrate those memories and the joy of the season."
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the Old World Christmas Royal Dansk ornament? It's a hand-crafted glass Christmas ornament shaped after Royal Dansk's iconic blue Danish Butter Cookies tin. Old World Christmas mouth-blows and hand-paints each one.
Where can I buy the Royal Dansk ornament? The ornament is available at OldWorldChristmas.com and Amazon in time for the 2026 holiday season.
How much does the Royal Dansk ornament cost? $27.99
Why did Royal Dansk and Old World Christmas partner up? Royal Dansk's blue tin is one of the most recognizable cookie tins around, and Old World Christmas has made glass ornaments since 1979.  Together, they turned a 60-year cookie tradition into a collectible ornament, with plans to expand the partnership.
Is the ornament made of glass? Yes. Like all Old World Christmas ornaments, it's mouth-blown from molten glass and hand-painted, using techniques inspired by 19th-century ornament-making.
When is the best time to buy it as a gift? It's a nostalgic pick for the 2026 holidays and pairs naturally with National Cookie Day on December 4. Order early, since these special partnership hand-crafted holiday ornaments tend to sell out.
About Old World Christmas Old World Christmas has made hand-blown glass ornaments since 1979. Each design is created in-house and handcrafted by skilled artisans, and the collection now spans more than 2,000 proprietary designs, from traditional to whimsical. Built to last and made to capture a memory, a milestone, a pet, or a person you love, the ornaments give everyone a way to tell the story of their lives one piece at a time. Learn more at www.oldworldchristmas.com .
About Royal Dansk Royal Dansk® Danish Butter Cookies have been elegantly crafted in Denmark since 1966, honoring traditional Danish baking from their origins in Helsingør. Produced exclusively in the Danish bakeries of Nørre Snede and Ribe, the cookies are made with real butter and contain no preservatives or artificial ingredients, staying true to the brand's commitment to quality. Royal Dansk offers a signature variety of artisanal cookie shapes, always presented in the iconic blue packaging. Keep up with the latest news at www.royal-dansk.com and on Facebook and Instagram .

The touchscreen MacBook has earned mythical creature status over the years, and we’re closing in on its debut, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. Apple is expected to launch 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros armed with touchscreen OLED panels sometime next month.
While we’ve already seen plenty of leaked info on the OLED MacBooks, Gurman’s latest report specifies that the new laptops will be “significantly lighter” than the current models. We don’t get a specific value, but according to the new report, Apple implemented a new internal component structure that has allowed them to shed weight. We expect the new laptops to feature Apple’s M6 chip . Apple is reportedly currently testing the new MacBook Pros with macOS 27.2 at the helm.
The new MacBook Pros won’t be the only devices getting an OLED upgrade. Apple is also expected to give the iPad mini a bump up to an OLED panel. It will likely feature the same 8.3-inch size, and there’s no word on a redesign.
I mean if they toned it down (which they would have to, if nothing else because USB-C only does 240W) it's at least plausible. Probably wouldn't be a massive performance hit either as CPUs tend to scale really badly with power consumption.
Meh. They'll call it revolutionary and Apple fans will eat it up and say it's the first laptop with a touch screen that makes sense.
I wonder how much cheaper the nontouch version will be.

articles.title_orig: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.title_zh: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.content_orig:
Supreme Court justices will begin hearing oral arguments Monday on a wide range of cases this term involving gun rights, religious freedom, immigration detention and the limits of government power.
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with cases that could reshape religious liberty, gun rights, immigration and the balance between state and federal authority.
While the last term was dominated by major cases testing presidential power — including Trump’s authority to restrict birthright citizenship, impose tariffs and fire independent agency officials — many of the court’s marquee cases this term span a wide range of issues, including federalism and individual rights.
"There’s a couple of religious freedom cases," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, told Fox News Digital. "We have a couple cases that touch on state and federal preemption, but I’m not sure there’s an easy theme for all of them."
The blockbuster case this term is Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, and it centers on whether Colorado officials can use state tort law to seek damages from oil giants Suncor and ExxonMobil for climate-related harms, or whether federal law blocks those claims.
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with major cases involving executive power, gun rights, religious liberty and voting rules. (Photo by Leah Millis-Pool/Getty Images)
SUPREME COURT CLIMATE SHOWDOWN JOLTED BY ALITO'S LAST-MINUTE DECISION
"If Colorado actually succeeds on its nuisance claims and others against these companies, the upshot would not just be these companies changing what they do in a way to protect Colorado or remedy Colorado, but rather it would affect their operations far outside of the state," Adam White, senior fellow at American Enterprise Institute, shared during a Federalist Society Panel. "And the question is, can Colorado courts reach outside of their own state and try in effect to regulate?"
Suncor and ExxonMobil argue that the Clean Air Act gives the federal government authority over interstate and international emissions, leaving Colorado unable to hold them liable for conduct outside the state. But the state argues that it is seeking damages under state law and that the Clean Air Act preserves states’ authority to enforce their own laws.
The Supreme Court will decide whether federal law blocks Boulder’s climate lawsuit and whether the justices can hear the case.
Severino said the case is an effort by "climate lawfare activists" to regulate carbon emissions.
"If the court is viewing this as an effort to weaponize one jurisdiction's law to really regulate outside its borders, then I think they're going to be not very happy about this claim," Severino said. "If the court really views it as an attempt by Colorado to legislate worldwide actions of these energy companies, then I think they're going to say this is actually something that fits within the federal government's sphere of activity, not a single state."
The case marks the first oral arguments heard before the high court.
An Arizona election integrity measure is at the center of another Supreme Court case testing the balance of power between states and the federal government over how elections are run.
Smith & Wesson M&P-15 semi-automatic rifles of the AR-15 style are displayed during the National Rifle Association (NRA) annual meeting at the George R. Brown Convention Center, in Houston, Texas, on May 28, 2022. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)
THESE 11 UPCOMING SUPREME COURT DECISIONS COULD MAKE OR BREAK TRUMP'S SECOND TERM AGENDA
Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota stems from an Arizona law requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship for certain voter registrations. Voters who register without that documentation may qualify as "federal-only" voters, allowing them to vote in federal elections but not state and local races. The law also allows the state to purge noncitizens off voter rolls close to an election. The dispute centers on whether the National Voter Registration Act prevents Arizona from imposing additional requirements on voters.
The Supreme Court will also hear major cases involving gun rights and religious liberty and will determine how far states can go in limiting those freedoms.
Colorado is up to bat twice before the Supreme Court this term, with St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy testing whether the state can exclude Catholic preschools from its universal preschool program because of religious policies barring same-sex couples and LGBT students from attending the schools, which conflicts with the state’s nondiscrimination requirements.
Colorado provides funding to private preschools that participate in the program but requires them to follow state anti-discrimination rules covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The Catholic schools argue those rules clash with their religious beliefs and that they should not have to abandon their policies to receive the same funding available to other private schools.
"They don't agree with the state on things like allowing children to use the opposite sex bathroom if they identify with the opposite sex. So this is something the Supreme Court has been very favorable to religious organizations of and for not allowing states to just cut them out of otherwise generally applicable state benefit programs," Severino said.
The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-world country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)
EXCLUSIVE: SUPREME COURT PRAYER GROTTO CASE COULD IMPACT 'EVERY SINGLE ZONING LAW' IN AMERICA, ATTORNEY SAYS
But Amanda Shanor, an attorney who helped represent the gay couple who were denied a wedding cake before the Supreme Court, said during a Federalist Society Panel there is concern that the case could chip away at anti-discrimination protections by expanding when businesses and institutions can refuse to serve people based on their identity.
"The schools are not saying, like in the earlier cases — like Masterpiece Cake Shop or 303 Creative — that they want to not serve somebody because of the expression that it would express with regard to a particular event, but instead that they don’t want to have the kids or the families because of the status of the kids or the families," Shanor said. "And will that then go spread over into other things, like will the bakery be able to say, ‘I don’t want to serve all X type of people?’"
Illinois and Connecticut have cases, with state laws restricting certain semiautomatic firearms facing challenges at the Supreme Court.
Members of the Supreme Court pose for a group photo at the Supreme Court on Oct. 7, 2022. Seated from left: Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Associate Justice Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice of the United States John G. Roberts Jr., Associate Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Associate Justice Elena Kagan. Standing behind from left: Associate Justice Amy Coney Barrett, Associate Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Associate Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
"This is important because the Supreme Court, for the first time following its landmark Bruen decision, is going to be looking at how states or municipalities can limit particular types of weapons," Severino said. "What the court said it's going to look at is whether these are weapons that are in common use and have lawful purposes, and so this is the court's opportunity to look at things like the popular AR-15 type rifle and decide is this something that qualifies as something that's in common-use and therefore is protected by the Second Amendment."
And while presidential power may not be a major theme this term, the Supreme Court will still weigh the limits of the Trump administration’s authority in a case involving its push to deport illegal immigrants to third-world countries they are not from, and that are not listed in their removal orders.

Dietary patterns worldwide have shifted toward increased consumption of ultraprocessed foods (UPFs), which has been linked to higher disease burden. One proposed mechanism underlying both UPF consumption and metabolic disease is altered post-ingestive responses relative to nutritionally similar foods. Here we report the effects of food processing on post-ingestive metabolism and brain response in a randomized, crossover study involving 57 healthy-weight adults who consumed a nutritionally matched UPF or non-UPF meal. We show that despite being nutritionally similar, UPF meals evoke greater insulinaemic and energetic responses, with attenuated carbohydrate oxidation relative to non-UPF meals. Between-condition differences in peak carbohydrate oxidation are associated with striatal activation in response to food cues. We also find that although subjective food value does not differ between conditions, brain responses correlated with food valuation are positive for non-UPF but negative for UPF in the visual cortex and striatum. Overall, these findings suggest that food processing influences post-ingestive metabolic and neural responses through mechanisms beyond calories and macronutrients alone.
The modern food environment has undergone a shift towards widespread availability of UPFs 1 , 2 . Under the Nova classification system, UPFs are industrially manufactured products that undergo multiple physical and chemical transformations and typically contain added industrial ingredients, specifically additives not commonly used in home cooking 3 . Concerningly, higher UPF intake is associated with poorer health outcomes, including cancer, overweight and obesity, and metabolic dysfunction 4 , 5 . Despite these adverse health associations, UPFs comprise the majority of calories consumed in the United States and most of the food market 1 , 2 . Although the mechanistic basis for UPF-associated health effects is not fully established, the incorporation of manufacturing processes that alter nutritional availability has been proposed as a potential factor 5 .
Even with the same ingredients, micronutrient bioavailability differs after food processing 6 . For macronutrients, industrial extrusion divides starches to produce a spectrum of fractions, granules and crystalline structures, augmenting digestibility and resulting in distinct glycaemic and insulinaemic properties 7 . For example, compared with steel-cut, instant oats that have been cooked at higher temperatures to partially gelatinize the starch elicit a higher glycaemic index despite still only containing oats 8 . Varying the cellular microstructure of chickpeas, including disrupting cell walls as seen in many UPFs, produced larger postprandial glucose and insulin excursions and greater concentrations of glucose and maltose in the duodenum 9 . Although evidence that food processing could lead to altered metabolic function is accumulating, much of it comes from studies that did not explicitly test foods that differ on the Nova score while controlling for nutritional composition.
If UPFs elicit augmented physiological responses owing to altered nutritional availability relative to nutritionally matched foods that are not ultraprocessed, not only could this provide a potential mechanism for their effects on metabolic health but also may represent a key mechanism contributing to their overconsumption. Foods high in both fat and sugar, as seen in many UPFs, are valued more than foods high in fat or sugar alone and elicit responses in regions critical for reward valuation, such as the striatum 10 , 11 . Moreover, this difference in food value is thought to be learned in part through gut-to-brain signalling driven by post-ingestive metabolic responses, known as flavour-nutrient learning 12 , 13 , 14 . The magnitude of the post-ingestive metabolic response to sugar-sweetened beverages has been associated with changes in rated liking and food-cue reactivity in the striatum, evidence for flavour-nutrient learning in humans 15 , 16 . This nutrient information is thought to be relayed from the duodenum, where nutrients cross the brush-border membrane, to the brain 17 , 18 , 19 . Collectively, these findings support a framework in which UPFs may amplify gut-to-brain signalling by increasing nutrient exposure at the proximal small intestine, the site of greatest nutrient absorption 19 , and leading to changed food valuation and consumption 12 , 13 , 20 .
To test this hypothesis, we characterized the post-ingestive response to nutrient-matched meals that differed in level of processing according to the Nova classification system. Next, we tested whether these processing-related differences in post-ingestive metabolism are associated with neural responses to food pictures and subjective food value. These findings identify potential post-ingestive mechanisms for overconsumption of foods, including UPFs, that extend beyond caloric and macronutrient composition alone.
The full study comprised 57 participants; of these, 32 completed both metabolic sessions in a randomized crossover design and 52 completed the functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) session (Extended Data Fig. 1 ). Every participant who completed the metabolic sessions also completed the fMRI session. The overall participant sample was 31.6% male, with a mean age of 26.21 ± 6.85 years and body mass index (BMI) of 22.75 ± 1.87 kg m −2 (Extended Data Table 1 ). Participants’ habitual energy intake on average comprised 54.4 ± 18.4% UPFs, similar to the national average of 55.0% (ref. 2 ). Additional participant characteristics are described in Extended Data Table 1 . Exclusions and final analytic samples for each modality are summarized in the CONSORT diagram (Extended Data Fig. 1 ).
To investigate the effect of processing level on post-ingestive metabolic response to foods with matched nutrient content, 32 participants consumed, and were required to finish within 10 min, ~300 kcal nutritionally matched meals composed entirely of either UPF or non-UPF while undergoing 4 h (50 min baseline followed by a 3 h postprandial period) of whole-room indirect calorimetry (WRIC) and concomitant blood collection by intravenous catheter (Fig. 1a ). The non-UPF and UPF test meals were closely matched on meal weight, energy, energy density, macronutrients, available carbohydrate, glycaemic index and load, total dietary fibre, sodium and water (all ≤1.6% deviation between meals; Fig. 1b ). The meals were consumed on separate days in a randomized crossover design, allowing within-participant comparison of indirect calorimetry and blood-derived metabolic outcomes (see Methods for session timing).

articles.title_zh: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
articles.content_orig:
The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.
The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.
He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia.
Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster".
More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight – whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami – emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated.
Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport.
He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX – with more than 180 passengers on board – into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports.
The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government.
The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board.
There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities.
UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure.
Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines.
But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency.
Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel".
Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017.

articles.title_orig: Emmanuel Macron is most impressive world leader on AI, says Sam Altman
articles.title_zh: Emmanuel Macron is most impressive world leader on AI, says Sam Altman
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI’s Sam Altman named French President Emmanuel Macron as the world leader who stands out for their approach to AI in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO .
“The person that came to mind as you were saying that is the French president,” Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon in response to being asked who has impressed him the most with their AI policy or plans for the technology.
“I think [Macron] is extremely thoughtful and has been for a long time about where this is going and what the shape of it needs to look like,” Altman said.
The recognition is notable because Macron has sought to use his leadership to push AI safety on the global stage, and because the French president is months away from leaving office.
After two terms as president, Macron is barred from running in the next election in April 2027. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls , is advocating a policy of deregulation on AI, three senior party officials told POLITICO .
Le Pen's National Rally party also wants to become less dependent on foreign tech companies and is considering reviving a proposal for a sovereign wealth fund to channel money toward French tech leaders such as OVH or Mistral, as well as favoring French companies in public contracts.
Some party figures have even threatened to repatriate French capital invested in American tech — €80 billion, according to party official Alexandre Loubet — without specifying how.
Macron himself has been a major champion of the French AI lab Mistral . Next month he’ll host the annual Paris Peace Forum — one of his pet diplomatic projects — to focus on AI safety and the risks technology poses to children and teenagers.
The Altman interview appears in Monday’s debut edition of Decoded by POLITICO and its accompanying daily podcast, covering global technology and focused on the personalities, political shifts and policy battles shaping the future of the world.
Read the full Decoded newsletter for more.

articles.title_orig: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.title_zh: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.content_orig:
After a volcano erupted on tiny Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, the 264 displaced islanders told the BBC about their first taste of modern British life.
"Just over a year ago, they'd never seen traffic or a road or a house higher than a cottage," said Tim Brinton in a 1963 BBC programme. He was talking about the residents of Tristan da Cunha, the world's most remote inhabited island. In the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly halfway between Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, the tiny British outpost is more than 1,500 miles from any other populated land, and is only accessible by a seven-day boat journey.
But on 10 October 1961, a sudden volcanic eruption blasted the islanders out of their splendid isolation and into the industrialised modern world. "We heard the rumbles first, then the ground just automatically cracked… Then the smoke and the fire started coming out the ground," one of them told the BBC in a 1998 film. Another, Mary Swain, said that she'd run to her husband and shouted, "Jump up quick, Fred, the Earth is opening!"
The island's volcano had been dormant since Tristan was first settled 150 years earlier. But great cracks appeared in the ground a few hundred metres from the main village, which is named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. By the time the islanders had escaped in their fishing boats to nearby Nightingale Island, their homes were already threatened by lava. "The whole place is vibrating with earthquakes," announced a BBC reporter, "and the eastern corner is cracking and breaking up."
Tristan's 264 inhabitants were forced to evacuate , picked up by a Dutch liner that happened to arrive the next day. Within hours, the whole community was aboard, leaving everything apart from the few things they could carry with them – "a rifle, an overcoat and a lamp," recalled Swain – and their boats, which they stored in their gardens when they reached England weeks later.
They were housed on a disused military airbase near Southampton, a port city on England's south coast. "So much is strange to them," said Brinton. "They'd never seen shops because on the island, money wasn't used. Boats were their livelihood. For them, there's been no industrial revolution. And for 150 years, they've lived simple agricultural lives out of touch with world progress."
Though Tristan da Cunha was discovered in 1506 by a Portuguese admiral who gave it his name, it was another 300 years before it supported anything but seabirds and seals. The UK annexed the island in 1816 to prevent it being used as a base for attempts to free Napoleon Bonaparte from his imprisonment on the South Atlantic island of St Helena . The following year, a Scotsman, Corporal William Glass, stayed behind when the British garrison was withdrawn. With his family and a few others, he founded the first permanent community.
In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter.
By 1961, the population of the 40 sq miles (100 sq km) of volcanic rock had risen to 264, many of them survivors from ships wrecked on the island, with just seven family names between them. On several occasions, the failure of the potato crop or the wrecking of fishing boats brought the islanders to the point of starvation. But they stayed on, even defying several attempts by the British government to evacuate them.
When the volcanic eruption forced the islanders to leave, they faced difficulties settling in England. They had never seen a car, a bicycle, a TV set or an income tax form. And it was a challenging climate. "Here is too much gas and smoke," Tristanian Joey Repetto told the BBC in 1963. On his journey to their initial accommodation, he said, "I steady coughed without stopping."
Adapting to the nine-to-five work pattern also proved tricky for the community of farmers and fishermen. "Here, when you go to work in the morning, you've got one job. You've got to look forward all the whole week of getting up at the same time, going to the same place, doing the same work every day," said Joey's father Gerald, who was used to a more varied life determined by natural rhythms.
Similarly, financial pressures placed new demands on the islanders, as Swain explained. "In England, you need money for your living. But on Tristan, we don't. If we haven't got no money, well, we just go without it. It don't bother us at all… if I've got no money, I still can go out and get my own potatoes. I can still go and get my own fish."
She didn't hold back on expressing her views on British life. "We don't like the weather... There's too much sickness and we don't like the place at all."
• The tiny island seized by Britain to foil the USSR
• The greatest sailing rescue ever made
• Queen Elizabeth II's secret night out on VE Day
Despite having a single policeman on the island, who wore a British uniform, Tristan had almost no crime. The community was shocked by an incident in England when one member was attacked and hurt by two youths, who took his most valued possession, a gold watch, and smashed it.
But there were some elements of British life that were appreciated by the Tristanians, particularly the younger ones, who described a love of Italian suits and record players. "Country and western music is our favourite, by Johnny Cash and Ernest Tubb," said one teenager, who also enjoyed the social dances. "Since I come here, I've been doing the twist and the locomotion, all that lot. We've forgotten how to do the waltz. But I like to twist myself."
Despite that, most of the islanders were keen to return home. In 1962, the British government sent a survey party to study conditions on Tristan. While the volcano was still smoking, the geologists judged that it was now dormant.
Surprisingly little damage had been done to the village of Edinburgh. The lava had turned at the last moment and flowed into the sea, something that the islanders considered to be an act of God. Some of the thatched roofs were burnt, but the cottages were mostly intact. Yet in their absence, houses had been ransacked and some livestock stolen by passing sailors.
Many animals were still alive, however, with the chickens multiplying in number. Though the dogs had run wild and slaughtered the sheep, the cattle had kept themselves well-fed on the lush island grass, and there were new calves. Lava had covered the beaches, but return was possible.
The British authorities held a secret ballot in the community hall at the islanders' RAF camp. All Tristanians over the age of 21 voted, and the result was an almost unanimous vote to return, 148 to five in favour. After an advance party went back to plant seeds for the following year's potato crop, most of the islanders arrived at Tristan da Cunha in November 1963.
When asked what she was most looking forward to on the island when she returned, Swain told the BBC: "A free life. We can get our own fish and everything of our own back there without money."
Elaine Repetto, who was born on the island but chose to leave in 1984, told the BBC in 1998 why it held such a pull. "We are strongly independent and used to battling with the elements in order to survive… We have to rely upon each other in a way you would find in few other places."
She described the impact of the events in 1961. "Today, the volcano is still a smoking reminder of the events which shaped our view of ourselves and our contact with the outside world."

articles.title_orig: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.title_zh: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.content_orig:
UCSF’s $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital is scheduled to open in 2030, but it wont’t fix the university’s staffing crisis, write Drs. Akshar Rambachan and Anand Habib.
Every day, we watch our patients and fellow physicians pay the price for a strained system we didn’t build and can’t fix alone.
We are doctors at UCSF. At UCSF’s flagship Parnassus Hospital, people sick enough to need a hospital room wait on gurneys in emergency-room hallways because there aren’t enough staffed hospital beds.
We see patients attached to IV antibiotics laying on beds outside ER bathrooms. Elderly patients with hip fractures and pain languish under bright lights and constant noise until, deprived of sleep, they develop delirium. Families are forced to discuss end-of-life wishes within earshot of strangers in the hallway.
These are the daily realities at what should be a world-class health-care system. It’s a patient-care crisis driven by a dysfunctional system that we, as doctors, had no hand in building — or get a say in changing.
For generations, doctors had the authority and independence to make structural staffing choices to deliver high-quality patient care. Physicians owned practices, allowing them to control their patient load and shape the staffing team.
That world is disappearing. Physicians increasingly work as employees of sprawling health systems in which decisions about staffing, workload, compensation and budgets are made further and further from the bedside.
Whatever the administrators are doing clearly isn’t working. UCSF’s emergency wait time is more than 20% higher than the national average .
When UCSF patients are finally seen, their average length of patient stay is 60% higher than the state average — which strongly correlates with negative patient outcomes .
The Parnassus ER has more than double the national average of patients who leave without seeing doctors.
As doctors, we write emails, join committees, conduct studies and share proposals shaped by our years of training, research and experience to address this crisis. Our reports, requests, complaints and proposals are treated as suggestions and all but ignored.
That is why we and physicians across the University of California system are organizing a union.
She’s a longtime Democratic officeholder, but she sounds like a Main Street conservative in her campaign for the state’s No. 2 job
Following concerns over how sensitive information is accessed, mayor’s new rules would shorten data retention, require documented searches and add oversight
Annual celebration of the US Navy is zooming back into The City for seven days of festivities and the return of the elite flight squad
UCSF’s solution to the patient care crisis is the $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital, scheduled to open in 2030. Let us be clear — we support the new hospital. Parnassus needs more critical inpatient and emergency rooms, and our patients deserve modern facilities.
But fancy new buildings don’t treat patients — people do. The expansion can’t be a substitute for solving the real crisis: the decreased investment in frontline staffing, resulting in chronic shortages that make it impossible to provide patients with world-class care.
We are often told that capital spending and staffing come from different budgetary “pots.” The accounting may separate capital and operating expenses, but the underlying finances are interconnected. UC’s own debt policy makes that clear: Medical centers seeking external financing must demonstrate adequate operating income, cash on hand and the ability to cover their debt payments .
In other words, financing what UCSF builds for tomorrow depends on the operating performance of the health system today — which is to say, on the people doing the work.
You cannot grow a system by hollowing out the front-line workers who make it run. Commitments to adequate staffing, sustainable workloads, and retention of the people required to operate new hospitals should not be revisited every budget cycle, revocable with every change in leadership. They should be codified and fixed to maintain continuity and quality.
To deliver on our mission to do everything in our power to get the best outcomes for our patients, doctors need a say not only in how we provide care, but also in the conditions within which that care happens.
We need mechanisms to ensure sufficient staffing at all levels, guardrails on how technology is used in patient care, and safe worksites that support healthy outcomes for our patients — not wait times that cause suffering and worsen their symptoms.
Through the UC Physicians Committee, doctors across specialties and campuses are organizing with University Professional and Technical Employees union, alongside many of the pharmacists, therapists and other professionals we already work with every day.
Together, we can codify common-sense policies so that every part of a patient’s care team is set up for success.
The Helen Diller Hospital is a promise about what UCSF intends to be in 2030. The medical professionals caring for San Franciscans today deserve a binding voice in what it is now. A union is how we get one, so that the institution we’re proud to work for can be the one that its patients were promised.
Dr. Akshar Rambachan is a hospital-medicine physician at UCSF. Dr. Anand Habib is an internal-medicine physician at UCSF.

articles.title_orig: Google admits not every Android app runs great on Intel Googlebooks
articles.title_zh: Google admits not every Android app runs great on Intel Googlebooks
articles.content_orig:
‘A small handful’ of apps apparently need some ‘developer tuning.’
‘A small handful’ of apps apparently need some ‘developer tuning.’
Google has waited until the day its new Googlebook laptops hit the market to admit that Intel-based models may have issues running some Android apps.
Before now, Google has emphasized that the Android-based Googlebooks give owners access to the “entire Play Store library” of apps, along with some clever interactions with Android phones and tablets . Today, in a statement to Android Authority , it admitted that while every app is available, some may not offer smooth performance on every Googlebook.
The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box. Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio.
Google hasn’t said how many apps will have performance issues, or named any specific apps that may have problems.
Of the five Googlebook laptops that have gone on sale today, three — models from Acer, Asus, and Lenovo — run on x86 Intel chips. The Dell and HP models instead run on Qualcomm’s Arm-based Snapdragon processors, and so should have greater compatibility with every Android app. We’ll be testing all five Googlebooks across the Verge team, and will report back on specific issues we find.

articles.title_orig: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.title_zh: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.content_orig:
China’s state television CCTV News shared video footage on Sunday of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) counter-uncrewed aerial systems (C-UAS) units in training with laser weapons, integrated missile-gun systems and high-power microwave technology as a layered defence against hostile drones.
PLA troops conducted live-fire tactical drills involving multiple day and night scenarios, CCTV said, adding that radar was used to detect a “dense swarm of drones” at low altitude. The C-UAS units then used a combination of laser ‘dazzling’ and electromagnetic measures to disrupt the formation of the swarm. Interceptor drones were also deployed as well as anti-aircraft guns.
He Qing, a PLA serviceman quoted by CCTV, said the drills combined responses to different aerial threats with battlefield operations and the handling of unexpected situations in an unfamiliar, complex desert environment.

articles.title_orig: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.title_zh: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.content_orig:
Energy Transition / Private Equity & Venture Capital / Sustainable Finance
Kenny Fisher October 5, 2026
Industrial heat and power solution provider Antora Energy announced plans for a new Kansas- based 5.8 GWh thermal battery storage project, anticipated to become one of the largest battery storage systems in the world once completed, with backing from investors including Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Grok Ventures.
The new battery storage project will be based at renewable fuel producer Pratt Energy’s biorefinery in Pratt, Kansas. Alongside the new project announcement, Antora also announced an offtake agreement to supply around-the-clock energy to Pratt Energy.
Founded in 2018, California-based Antora develops thermal batteries that store low-cost electricity as heat in insulated blocks of solid carbon and deliver the stored energy around the clock as industrial heat or power.
The project’s third-party equity financing was led by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) as part of its credit platform investments, and included participation from Australian climate-focused investment firm Grok Ventures and University Pension Plan Ontario (UPP).
Reiner Boehning, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said:
“Antora has demonstrated something rare: sound technology, compelling economic fundamentals, and a clear path to repeatable deployment at scale. That gave us the conviction to partner with Antora on this project.”
Under the new offtake agreement, Antora will supply energy from the 5.8 GWh thermal battery system to Pratt Energy beginning in 2027. The battery will store low-cost electricity as heat in solid carbon blocks and supply that heat continuously to the biorefinery. The companies said that the project will improve Pratt’s operational efficiency and product competiveness, as well as supporting the company’s efforts toward producing 100% zero-carbon-intensity (CI) ethanol.
David Bierman, co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Antora, said:
“Our partnership with Pratt Energy delivers it, helping meet Kansas’s rising energy demand without increasing power bills for homes or businesses. This biorefinery project is creating jobs and spurring local investment without straining the resources the community depends on.”

articles.title_orig: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.title_zh: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”.
Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming.
It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets.

articles.title_orig: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.title_zh: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s Washington may be about to get the Brazil it wants, a major piece of the hemispheric puzzle falling into place for the so-called “Donroe Doctrine. "
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, took 47 percent of the valid vote on Sunday to left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45 percent, setting up an October 25 runoff .
Trump has not formally endorsed him , but a Bolsonaro win would give the U.S. its friendliest government in Brasília since the elder Bolsonaro’s, just as Washington tries to loosen China’s grip on strategic supply chains.
China will look on nervously, but much of its groundwork in Brazil is already laid. Those foundations will be tough to break, even with a Trump-friendly Bolsonaro government in power.
The trade data shows why. In the first eight months of this year, Brazil exported $77.1 billion in goods to China, up 15 percent year-on-year, compared to just $24.1 billion to the U.S. , down 9.7 percent. That is a ratio of more than 3-to-1.
Two-way trade with China reached $128.6 billion, against $51.4 billion with the U.S. Brazil’s soybean sales to China alone outstripped everything it sold to America. And the gap is widening. A year earlier, the ratio was 2.5-to-1.
Brazil is physically closer to the U.S. and sits in the hemisphere over which Trump is asserting American hegemony. But Brasília is, in many ways, closer to Beijing than Washington.
To be sure, a Bolsonaro victory would be a real prize for Trump. But political alignment cannot repeal economic geography.
A new president can reset Brazil’s diplomatic posture in January. He cannot, at the wave of a hand, reroute the 305 million metric tons of cargo Brazil shipped to China in those eight months.
Trade on that scale doesn’t make Brazil China’s ally, though they are partnered through the BRICS bloc. But it means Beijing’s leverage depends less on who governs Brasília than on the material reality of who buys Brazil’s harvests and processes its minerals.
For evidence, look at Bolsonaro’s coalition. Brazil’s congressional farm caucus endorsed him days before the vote, and Mato Grosso, the heart of soy country, gave him about 65 percent .
Roughly 70 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports from January through August went to China. Washington cannot replace the Chinese customer. It competes with Brazil for it.
Trump’s 2025 deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping commits Beijing to buy at least 25 million metric tons of American soybeans a year through 2028. And since July, Washington has imposed a 25 percent tariff on most Brazilian goods .
Brazil has run this experiment before. Ahead of his 2018 election, Jair Bolsonaro visited Taiwan and accused China of buying Brazil . By October 2019, he was in Beijing , courting Chinese investment.
Over his term, trade with China grew, his government resisted U.S. pressure to shut Huawei out of Brazil’s 5G network entirely, and Brazil stayed in BRICS.
Rare earths, command of which will decide the great power competition in the 21 st century, make matters worse.
The younger Bolsonaro told CPAC in Texas in March that Brazil would be “the battleground where the future of the hemisphere will be fought,” and said he discussed rare earths with Trump in the Oval Office in May.
Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves but produced less than 1 percent of global output last year. The chokepoint isn’t the mine, but the refinery.
And here’s the difficult truth: China and Chinese-controlled firms handled 91 percent of the world’s rare-earth processing in 2024.
Pela Ema, a mine in the state of Goiás, is Washington’s showcase. About $5 billion in U.S.-backed loans, acquisition money, and price guarantees is converging on it, and last month a U.S. company bought its owner , Serra Verde.
Yet the mine yields only a mixed carbonate, an intermediate product. Separating its heavy rare earths requires a route the U.S. has not proved at commercial scale, so some output may be stockpiled.
Meanwhile, the company’s legacy contracts with Chinese processors run until the end of this year.
All of it unfolded on Lula’s watch, not a Bolsonaro. Washington’s push for Pela Ema was built on capital and guaranteed prices. No presidential sympathy needed.
What Washington still lacks is processing. No Brazilian president can conjure that. The reality is that America will rely on China for rare earths well into the 2030s .
Trump’s own January proclamation warned that even domestic mining does not safeguard national security if the U.S. “remains dependent on a foreign country for the processing.”
Washington’s has time, and it can move quickly. It assembled most of the Pela Ema package within months, and substantial new heavy-rare-earth separation capacity outside China is a few years away , roughly one Brazilian presidential term.
A Bolsonaro government could fast-track permits, court U.S. capital for new deposits, and deliver what Fernanda Magnotta of the Inter-American Dialogue expects: “ greater screening of investments in sensitive sectors .”
Pair that with U.S. tariff relief, and by 2030 Brazil could anchor a Western rare-earth supply chain even as its soybeans keep sailing to China.
The runoff can change the U.S.-China contest in Brazil without settling it. What happens next will take shape by the end of a Bolsonaro term, assuming, as all indications suggest, he will triumph in the next round.
If China’s share of Brazil’s exports, about 31 percent so far this year , has fallen below a quarter, Pela Ema’s heavy rare earths are being separated outside China at scale, and Chinese capital is screened out of strategic assets, then Washington won Brazil outright.
But if not, Trump won the palace and lost the ports.

articles.title_orig: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.title_zh: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.content_orig:
China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country.
Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis.
Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report , which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less-developed regions of the country.
The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, non-performing loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles.
The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to system-wide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure.
The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added.
The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy.
China's GDP grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.

Spanish PM Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election days after Congress voted against measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis
SÃ¡nchez's government had presented the measures in response to nationwide protests, triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home for failing to pay a sharp rent increase
The woman's rent was raised from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since 2018. Spain was not due to hold a general election until summer 2027 - here's what happened last time
Most polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election, which will take place on 29 November
SÃ¡nchez clearly wants to take the initiative - but it's going to be very tough for him to remain in power, writes Guy Hedgecoe in Madrid
Edited by Rorey Bosotti and Imogen James
Dan Woodland Live reporter
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election on 29 November, bringing forward the vote which was originally scheduled for the summer of 2027.
The move follows weeks of protests across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants, sparked last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid following a sharp rent increase.
SÃ¡nchezâs leftist coalition government failed to pass emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis on Friday - but is now expected to approve measures on Tuesday.
The premier's position has also been marred by multiple corruption investigations in recent months involving former members of government and even his wife and brother.
Opposition parties welcomed the snap election, with the leader of the conservative People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o declaring Spain will "at last" say "what it thinks", and leader of the far-right Spanish party Vox Santiago Abascal saying he was "glad" about the announcement.
Meanwhile, members of SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians expressed confidence that they would be re-elected and the prime minister would "pull off a comeback".
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next vote, however they would be expected to need Vox's support to form a government.
This will be SÃ¡nchez's sixth election in 11 years, and if he is to remain in power, he needs to upset some tough odds, writes our reporter in Madrid .
We're ending our live coverage here, but you can read more in our news story .
With eight years in power, Pedro SÃ¡nchez is now Spain's second longest-serving prime minister in recent history.
His political career has been marked by dramatic twists and turns, including his resignation as Socialist Party leader in 2016 after losing the support of senior party figures. Just seven months later, he staged a remarkable comeback, returning to the leadership with the backing of grassroots members.
SÃ¡nchez has called an early election despite opinion polls suggesting he may struggle to secure enough support to remain in power.
Some analysts believe that focusing the campaign on Spain's housing crisis could help mobilise left-wing voters and steer the debate away from other challenges facing the government, including the situation in Ceuta and corruption allegations involving figures close to SÃ¡nchez.
It is not the first time SÃ¡nchez has taken a major political gamble. In 2023, he called a snap election after his party suffered heavy losses in regional and local elections.
Polls at the time also suggested he was heading for defeat.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, SÃ¡nchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to stay in office, thanks to agreements with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Opposition parties accused him of "selling out Spain" in order to remain in power.
The High Court of Justice of Madrid has rejected a request to disperse an encampment in Puerto Del Sol in the Spanish capital.
Protesters have set up tents in the famous square since 27 September, court documents show.
The court rejected the Community of Madrid's request for police to clear the square on Monday. A new hearing is expected to take place on Wednesday.
A trade union has also called on people to continue protesting in the street against issues with wages and housing ahead of the snap election.
The general secretary of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) trade union confederation, Unai Sordo, says: "We must continue with a path of mobilisation, of street protests as we had announced, regarding wages and housing measures, and that will be our course in the coming months."
People in the streets of Madrid say they welcome news of the snap election called by Prime Minister SÃ¡nchez this morning.
âI think itâs good given the situation thatâs arisen", Raomon Diaz tells Reuters.
"Young people have been given little prospect for the future. And Iâd like to see a truly left-wing government finally come to power.â
Protester Florencio Diaz described the election announcement as a "great victory for the protests in the streets".
Florencio Diaz says Spanish people are struggling with the cost of living
"Weâre in a very difficult situation, with the cost of living rising and, above all, the abuse taking place in the housing market", he says.
However, Sandra - who is also protesting against Spain's housing crisis - expressed reservations about what the future holds.
âTo be honest, Iâm a bit worried about what might happen. But itâs certainly true that with the government we have, things arenât moving forward.â
Sandra says she's worried about Spain's future
The Spanish government is expected to approve measures on Tuesday aimed at tackling the housing crisis that parliament rejected last week .
The measures include a suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030 and an automatic renewal of rental contracts.
The government failed to pass them last week, after they were opposed by the People's Party (PP), Vox, and Junts.
Once the government approves the measures, SÃ¡nchez has 30 days to get them ratified. But the Madrid-based political newspaper Moncloa suggests that the prime minister's calling of a snap election could help him do this without congress, as parliament will be dissolved before those 30 days are up.
When congress isn't sitting, ratifying the measures falls to a committee which has a more favourable political make-up for SÃ¡nchez and doesn't require support from the Junts party, the newspaper says.
The deputy prime minister of Spain Yolanda DÃ­az has called for rent caps and a shortened workday
Members of Pedro SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians have continued to react to the Spanish snap election.
The deputy prime minister of Spain, Yolanda DÃ­az - who is part of the Sumar movement - says in a post on Bluesky: "We are going to win again."
DÃ­az says the group will cap rents, shorten the workday and raise the minimum wage.
Health minister MÃ³nica GarcÃ­a says in a post on X that the "Spanish people will rise to the occasion and prevail over the resentment of international hate".
Meanwhile Justice minister FÃ©lix BolaÃ±os says on X that the prime minister "will pull off a comeback" and leave the People's Party and Vox "without a government".
Catalan President Salvador Illa Roca says elections will be a "moment to decide between continuing to advance or going backwards". "Catalonia will stand with Pedro SÃ¡nchez," he adds.
SÃ¡nchez celebrates beside his wife Begona Gomez, after winning the general elections in 2019
These will be the sixth elections that Pedro SÃ¡nchez has contested as Socialist leader since 2015.
He has only won two of those - the 2019 ballot which was repeated after being inconclusive - and yet he has been in power since winning a no-confidence motion against his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy, in 2018.

articles.title_orig: A Trump-sized shadow looms over the Supreme Court's new term
articles.title_zh: A Trump-sized shadow looms over the Supreme Court's new term
articles.content_orig:
Type to search articles, cases, and authors.
Press ↵ to view all results.
The first Monday in October brings the new Supreme Court term and, with it, the first day of oral arguments.
The opening case is Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County , on whether state-tort claims against energy companies brought by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, are preempted by federal law. It’s a big case, with potentially significant implications.
Before argument begins, Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s wife, Ashley Kavanaugh, and his parents, Everett and Martha Kavanaugh, arrive to take seats in the justices’ guest box.
Also here are three Boulder County commissioners – Ashely Stolzmann, Marta Loachamin, and Claire Levy, as well as Boulder City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde. They will make brief remarks to the press on the court’s plaza after the arguments. Here as well are Suncor General Counsel Mike Korenblat and ExxonMobil General Counsel Jeffrey Taylor. They will not go to the plaza.
At 10 a.m., the justices take the bench, except for Justice Samuel Alito, of course. He announced last week that he would no longer participate in Suncor . Some advocacy groups had called for his recusal based on his ownership of individual energy stocks, though not of Suncor or ExxonMobil.
Alito told Bloomberg’s Greg Stohr last week, an interview tied to Tuesday’s release of his book “ So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country ,” that he felt it was “prudent” to withdraw even though the court’s legal office had advised him recusal was not required.
One question debated among a certain especially law-nerdy set of observers, possibly just a couple of us here at SCOTUSblog, was whether the court would switch the order of today’s cases because of the late recusal. The court’s preferred custom is that when a justice is recused and there is more than one case being argued in a day, the case with the recusal will go second so the non-participating justice can slip out relatively quietly in the short break between cases.
But Suncor was seemingly scheduled as a high-profile term opener (and touted as such in many a term preview session). The court evidently decided not to disrupt the narrative.
The chief justice opens with some traditional business: “I have the honor to announce, on behalf of the court, that the October 2025 Term of the Supreme Court of the United States is now closed, and the October 2026 Term is now convened.”
During bar admissions, one movant departs from the short, scripted motion to tout his “fellow Marine” who will “make a great ambassador for the court.” The chief justice does not seem amused by the ad lib.
Among the groups being admitted today are several graduates of the University of the District of Columbia’s David A. Clarke School of Law, where Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson last month received a raucous welcome for her speech and conversation about the emergency docket, and a group from the U.S. House office of legislative counsel, whose members’ ears will perk up during the Suncor arguments and its many mentions of the potential role of Congress in regulating greenhouse gas emissions.
Roberts then calls the Suncor case for “argument first this term.”
Amy Howe has this site’s main account of the argument. To me, it was clear from early on that the question presented that the court added to the case, about whether it has jurisdiction over a Colorado Supreme Court decision that arguably isn’t final, was more than just a formality.
Justice Clarence Thomas asks Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer representing Suncor and ExxonMobil, the defendants in Boulder city and county’s lawsuit, to “spend some time and explain why we have jurisdiction.”
Shanmugam was then forced to spend almost all of his allotted 20 minutes of traditional time on the jurisdiction question.
When Justice Elena Kagan suggests that he was switching back and forth between two theories of jurisdiction that were perhaps in tension with each other and so he should maybe choose one, Shanmugan says, “Like my children, I love both of our theories equally, Justice Kagan.”
She doesn’t seem amused and continues to press him.
Only when he gets to the seriatim round does Shanmugam get to expound on the merits, though this is after Roberts turns to Thomas, who has no further questions, and then reflexively turns to Alito’s chair (which also has no questions).
Before his time is up, Shanmugam is able to make a sweeping point that more than 60 municipalities across the country have filed some three dozen similar lawsuits seeking to hold oil and gas companies liable for damages related to greenhouse gas emissions.
“I would submit that, given the extraordinary magnitude of these cases, where, in each of these cases, plaintiffs are seeking billions of dollars of damages, that we need an answer to this question sooner rather than later,” he says.
Sarah Harris, the current principal deputy solicitor general arguing in support of the petitioners, argues that the Colorado Supreme Court treated the case as a self-contained original proceeding, and thus the U.S. Supreme Court has jurisdiction to review that court’s ruling allowing the lawsuit to proceed.
Kevin Russell, representing the two Boulders and their officials, makes a few merits points before saying, “all of this must await another case because petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal.”
Roberts, who had suggested to Harris that this suit may not be different from other mass tort suits the Supreme Court has allowed to proceed in state court, takes a more skeptical tone with Russell.
“If you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit—they’ll probably copy your pleadings—and then there will be at least 50, you know, different cities’ … causes of action filed,” the chief justice says. “[H]ow do you think that will work out on the ground?”
Russell responds calmly, giving a little but saying, “the mere fact that … there could be a lot of litigation, I don't think there’s anything in the Constitution that says preemption arises from whenever, you know, a state law, if copied in other states, could cause a lot of litigation.”
On rebuttal, Shanmugam takes one more stab at emphasizing the scope of the climate lawsuits that he is hoping the court will nip in the bud.
“The breadth of Boulder's theory here is astonishing,” he says, “[t]here is no limit under Boulder's theory on who could be sued.”
Under the lawsuit’s theory, he adds, “Boulder could tag me with personal jurisdiction when I am in Colorado in two weeks and sue me on a nuisance claim for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change.”
Shanmugam concludes by saying, “[T]his case and others like it reflect an all-too-regrettable trend of trying to resolve major political issues in court rather than leaving them to the political branches where they belong. Climate change is certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it.”
With that, Roberts says the case is submitted, and many in the courtroom stand to leave.
During this commotion, Alito slips in from the center curtain with a slight smile on his face and moves to his place on the bench. During the next argument , on veterans’ benefits , he will be back at home asking tough questions of counsel, rather than sitting around in his chambers, or perhaps worse, answering questions from news reporters, even if it is to promote his book.
Mark Walsh has covered the U.S. Supreme Court since 1991.

articles.title_orig: Why the PLA’s Z-10 attack helicopter is taking a bigger role at sea
articles.title_zh: Why the PLA’s Z-10 attack helicopter is taking a bigger role at sea
articles.content_orig:
Aircraft was built to hunt tanks and support ground troops, but a broader maritime role means it can operate closer to Taiwan
Manufactured by AVIC subsidiary the Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, the Z-10 entered service with the PLA Army in late 2010. It began documented shipboard trials in 2014, when Chinese navy imagery showed a Z-10 landing on the Baxianshan Type 072A tank landing ship.
The attack helicopter’s maritime role has gradually expanded since then. In 2020, army helicopters practised landing, refuelling and rearming on a civilian semi-submersible.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of French schools stay closed ahead of nationwide day of student protests
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of French schools stay closed ahead of nationwide day of student protests
articles.content_orig:
Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.
Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff".
He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent.
Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions.
